cau_hoi: Which American inventor is famous for the long-lasting incandescent light bulb that became widely available in 1879?
giai_thich: Edison was not the first to create the electric light bulb, but he and his team tested thousands of materials to find a durable filament, ultimately choosing carbonized bamboo that lasted over 1,000 hours. He also built an entire system of power plants and wiring to deliver electricity to homes. Throughout his life, Edison held over 1,000 patents in the U.S.

cau_hoi: Which invention, patented in 1876, allowed people to communicate over long distances via electrical wires?
giai_thich: Alexander Graham Bell, a Scottish-born inventor living in the U.S., was granted the patent for the telephone on March 7, 1876. The first words spoken over the phone were him calling his assistant in the next room: "Mr. Watson, come here, I need you." Both Bell's mother and wife were deaf, so he spent many years researching sound and teaching the hearing impaired.

cau_hoi: In 1903, which American brothers made the first controlled flight in a powered aircraft?
giai_thich: Orville and Wilbur Wright were originally bicycle mechanics. On December 17, 1903, in Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, the Flyer flew for 12 seconds covering 37 meters. They succeeded by solving the problem of controlling the aircraft's tilt and turn, something other inventors had not achieved. The Lumière brothers were filmmakers, and the Montgolfier brothers invented hot air balloons.

cau_hoi: Which ancient invention, appearing in the Mesopotamia region about 5,500 years ago, helped humans transport heavy goods more easily and is considered one of the most important inventions?
giai_thich: The first wheels were solid wooden discs used for carts and possibly for potter's wheels. The hardest part was not the wheel itself but the axle: the axle and hole had to fit snugly and smoothly for the wheel to turn evenly. Interestingly, the Maya and Aztec in the Americas knew how to make wheels for toys but did not use them for transporting goods, perhaps because they lacked large animals to pull them.

cau_hoi: What do we call a machine that can be programmed to work autonomously, such as vacuuming a house or assembling cars in a factory?
giai_thich: The term "robot" comes from the Czech word "robota," meaning forced labor. The first industrial robot, Unimate, began working at the General Motors factory in 1961, specializing in handling hot metal sheets. Today, robots are used in factories, hospitals, farms, and even on Mars as rovers.

cau_hoi: What invention is responsible for the oldest surviving photograph, taken from the window of Joseph Nicéphore Niépce's house in France around 1826?
giai_thich: Niépce coated a sheet of tin with a special asphalt that hardened when exposed to light. He had to leave the camera pointing out the window for many hours, possibly days, to capture a blurry image of the roof and courtyard. Consequently, in the photograph, sunlight shines on both sides of the building. Today, it only takes a fraction of a second to take a photo.

cau_hoi: In 1905, how did 11-year-old Frank Epperson accidentally create the popsicle?
A: Mixing ice with salt in a school experiment
B: Leaving fruit juice in a store's freezer
C: Forgetting a cup of soda with a stirring stick outside on a cold night
giai_thich: The next morning, Frank found the soda frozen around the stirring stick and took a bite. It wasn't until the early 1920s, when he was older, that he applied for a patent and sold the treat under the name "Epsicle," later changed to "Popsicle." This story shows that interesting inventions can come from a child's curiosity.

cau_hoi: The Rubik's Cube, one of the best-selling toys of all time, was invented in 1974 in which country?
giai_thich: Ernő Rubik was an architecture teacher in Budapest. He made the first cube from wood and rubber bands to help students understand three-dimensional space. It took him about a month to solve it for the first time. The 3×3 Rubik's Cube has over 43 quintillion possible combinations, but mathematicians have proven that any state can be solved in a maximum of 20 moves.

cau_hoi: In 1891, physical education teacher James Naismith invented basketball. What were the original "baskets"?
A: Iron hoops with nets like today
B: Peach baskets hanging from a railing
C: Fishing nets tied to a tree
D: A wooden box placed on the ground
giai_thich: Naismith needed an indoor sport for students to play during the cold winter in Springfield, USA. He hung two peach baskets at a height of about 3.05 meters, exactly the height of today's basketball hoop. Since the baskets still had bottoms, every time a point was scored, someone had to climb up to retrieve the ball. It wasn't until later that the bottoms of the baskets were cut out.

cau_hoi: How does a 3D printer create an object?
A: Pouring molten metal into a mold
C: Carving a large block into shape
D: Layering thin materials on top of each other according to a computer design
giai_thich: The most common 3D printers melt plastic filament and extrude it along a predetermined path, layer by layer, like building a house from the ground up. This technology was invented in the 1980s. Today, people can print toys, airplane parts, prosthetic limbs, and even concrete houses, and they are experimenting with printing living tissues in medicine.

cau_hoi: The LEGO building toy was founded by a carpenter in 1932 in which country?
giai_thich: Ole Kirk Christiansen initially made wooden toys. The name LEGO is derived from the Danish phrase "leg godt", meaning "play well". The modern plastic LEGO brick was patented in 1958 and can interlock with bricks produced from then until now. With just 6 bricks of 2×4 of the same color, over 915 million different combinations can be created.

cau_hoi: In 1752, which device did Benjamin Franklin invent to protect homes from lightning strikes?
giai_thich: Franklin believed that lightning was electricity, and a pointed metal rod placed on the roof, connected to the ground, could safely conduct the lightning's electrical charge to the ground. He did not patent it so that everyone could use it for free. The lightning rod was quickly installed on many buildings and church steeples, which were often struck by lightning.

cau_hoi: The Braille system for the visually impaired, using raised dots to read with the fingertips, was created by whom at around the age of 15?
giai_thich: Louis Braille became blind at the age of 3 due to an accident in his father's workshop. At a school for the blind in Paris, he learned about a military dot system used to read messages at night. He simplified it so that each letter consisted of a maximum of 6 dots in a small cell, fitting under the fingertip. In 1824, at just 15 years old, Braille completed this system, which is now used worldwide.

cau_hoi: In 1886, who was granted a patent for the gasoline-powered car, considered the first modern automobile?
giai_thich: The Benz Patent-Motorwagen had three wheels and could travel at about 16 km/h. In 1888, his wife Bertha Benz drove the car with their two sons about 106 km to visit her mother without informing her husband, marking the first long-distance journey by car, which helped promote the invention. Along the way, she had to buy gasoline at a pharmacy, as gasoline was sold as a cleaning solvent at that time.

cau_hoi: In 1931, which Hungarian journalist developed the ballpoint pen after noticing that newspaper ink dried very quickly?
giai_thich: Bíró noticed that newspaper ink was thick, dried quickly, and did not smudge, but it was too thick to flow through a fountain pen nib. Together with his brother, chemist György, he used a small ball at the tip of the pen that rotated while drawing ink from the tube onto the paper. He patented it in the UK in 1938, then fled to Argentina to escape the war and continued producing pens there. In many countries, ballpoint pens are still called "biro".

cau_hoi: In 1783, in France, who were the first "passengers" to fly in the Montgolfier brothers' hot air balloon in front of the king?
C: A sheep, a duck, and a rooster
giai_thich: No one knew if humans could survive at high altitudes, so the Montgolfier brothers experimented with animals. The balloon flew for about 8 minutes before landing safely; the sheep may have kicked the rooster, causing it minor injuries. Two months later, two Frenchmen became the first to fly in a hot air balloon, hovering over the Paris sky for about 25 minutes.

cau_hoi: In Morse code, how is the international distress signal "SOS" transmitted?
A: Three dots, three dashes, three dots
B: Three dashes, three dots, three dashes
giai_thich: Morse code was developed by Samuel Morse and Alfred Vail for the telegraph in the 1830s – 1840s, with each letter represented by a group of short signals (dots) and long signals (dashes). SOS was chosen in 1906 because it is very easy to remember and recognize, not because it stands for "Save Our Souls" as many people think. The Titanic sent an SOS signal when it encountered disaster in 1912.

cau_hoi: The modern "zipper" with two rows of small interlocking teeth was patented in 1917 by whom?
giai_thich: Swedish-American engineer Gideon Sundback designed a zipper with small cup-shaped teeth that interlock, using a slider to open and close it. Initially, zippers were used for rubber boots and cigarette cases. The English term "zipper" comes from the sound "zip" when pulling the zipper. It wasn't until the 1930s that zippers became popular in clothing.

cau_hoi: In 1926, Scottish inventor John Logie Baird demonstrated what for the first time?
giai_thich: Baird initially built the machine from inexpensive materials like hat boxes, sewing needles, bicycle lamps, and a rotating perforated disk to scan images. The first image was the face of a ventriloquist dummy named "Stooky Bill". His mechanical television was later replaced by electronic television, but he is still remembered as a pioneer.

cau_hoi: On April 3, 1973, engineer Martin Cooper at Motorola made the first call from a handheld mobile phone. Who did he call?
giai_thich: Cooper stood on the streets of New York and called Joel Engel, the head of the mobile phone group at Bell Labs, his competitor racing against Motorola, to "show off" that he had done it first. The DynaTAC phone weighed about 1.1 kg, was about 25 cm long, and charged for 10 hours, allowing for about 35 minutes of talk time.

cau_hoi: Which British computer scientist invented the World Wide Web in 1989 while working at CERN (Switzerland)?
giai_thich: Berners-Lee wanted scientists to easily share documents. He created the first website, the first web browser, and protocols like HTML, HTTP, and web addresses (URLs). He decided not to patent it so that everyone could use it for free. The Internet is a network connecting computers, while the World Wide Web is a system of information pages running on the Internet.

cau_hoi: What is different about the first "bicycle" invented by German Baron Karl Drais in 1817 compared to today's bicycles?
C: It was made entirely of iron
D: It had no pedals; the rider had to push their feet on the ground to propel it
giai_thich: Drais's wooden "running machine" was created after 1816, when a poor harvest caused many horses to starve, so people needed a horse-free means of transport. It wasn't until the 1860s that pedals were attached to the front wheel. Today, balance bikes without pedals for young children are descendants of this invention.

cau_hoi: Where and when was the first toothbrush with bristles similar to today's recorded, in 1498?
A: China, using pig bristles attached to a handle made of bamboo or bone
giai_thich: Previously, people brushed their teeth with sticks that had one end chewed to fray. The pig bristle toothbrush was brought from China to Europe. In 1938, DuPont created the first nylon bristle toothbrush, which was more durable and hygienic. Pigs in cold regions like Siberia had coarser hair and were thus preferred for making brushes.

cau_hoi: How long did the Wright brothers' first flight on December 17, 1903, last?
giai_thich: The Flyer, piloted by Orville, only flew about 37 meters, shorter than the wingspan of a modern Boeing 747 passenger plane. On that day, the brothers took turns flying four times, with the longest flight by Wilbur covering about 260 meters in 59 seconds. Just 66 years later, humans flew to the Moon.

cau_hoi: Where were reading glasses invented around the year 1286?
giai_thich: A sermon by monk Giordano da Pisa in 1306 mentions that glasses were invented about 20 years earlier, likely in the Pisa or Venice area, known for its glassmaking. The first glasses were two convex lenses mounted on a frame, resting on the nose without ear supports. Glasses helped scholars and craftsmen work for many more years as they aged.

cau_hoi: At the end of 1895, the Lumière brothers in France held the first ticketed film screenings. Legend has it that when watching a scene from one of their short films, the audience was terrified?
giai_thich: The short film "The Arrival of a Train at La Ciotat Station" is only about 50 seconds long, showing a train running straight towards the camera. According to legend, some audience members thought the train was about to crash out of the screen and ran away, although historians doubt this story has been exaggerated. The Lumière brothers' "Cinématographe" could film, print, and project movies.

cau_hoi: Which British mathematician designed the "analytical engine" in the 19th century, considered the first concept of a general-purpose computer?
giai_thich: Charles Babbage was frustrated with error-filled printed calculation tables, so he designed the "difference engine" for automatic calculations, followed by the "analytical engine" with memory, a processor, and instructions read from punched cards. He never completed the machine due to lack of funding and technology of the time. In 1991, the Science Museum in London built the difference engine No. 2 according to his designs, and it worked perfectly.

cau_hoi: Who is considered the "first programmer in history" for writing an algorithm for Babbage's analytical engine in 1843?
giai_thich: Ada Lovelace was the daughter of poet Lord Byron. When translating an article about the analytical engine, she added notes three times longer than the original, including a method for the machine to compute Bernoulli numbers. She also predicted that computers could do more than calculations, such as composing music if they knew how to encode sound. The programming language Ada is named after her.

cau_hoi: In 1873, 15-year-old Chester Greenwood in Maine (USA) invented what item because his ears were cold while ice skating?
giai_thich: Chester asked his grandmother to make pads out of beaver fur and velvet, attached to a bent steel wire frame. In 1877, he was granted a patent and opened a factory to produce ear warmers, supplying the U.S. military during World War I. The town of Farmington where he lived still holds "Chester Greenwood Day" every December.

cau_hoi: The trampoline was invented by two Americans around 1930; how old was George Nissen at that time, and what inspired him?
B: About 40 years old, while working in the military
C: About 8 years old, while jumping on a bed
D: About 16 years old, while watching acrobats fall onto a safety net in a circus
giai_thich: Nissen was a gymnast. Seeing acrobats bounce when they fell into the net, he and coach Larry Griswold created a steel frame stretched with canvas and springs. The name "trampoline" comes from the Spanish word "trampolín" (springboard). To promote it, Nissen once jumped on a trampoline with a kangaroo. Since 2000, trampoline has been an Olympic sport.

cau_hoi: During World War II, mathematician Alan Turing and his colleagues at Bletchley Park (UK) accomplished what important task?
A: Deciphered encrypted messages from Germany encoded by the Enigma machine
giai_thich: The Enigma machine could encode each letter in trillions of ways, and the Germans changed the settings every day. Turing designed the electromechanical machine 'Bombe' to find the settings much faster. Historians estimate that the deciphering efforts shortened the war by about two years. Turing is also considered the father of theoretical computer science; the highest award in computing is named after him.

cau_hoi: ENIAC, one of the first general-purpose electronic computers, was completed in 1946 in the USA. What was its size?
A: The size of a study desk
B: Occupied an entire large room, weighed about 27 tons with approximately 18,000 vacuum tubes
giai_thich: ENIAC was about 30 meters long and consumed about 150 kW of electricity. It was rumored that every time it was turned on, the street lights in Philadelphia dimmed. Programming ENIAC involved reconnecting hundreds of wires and flipping switches, a task handled by six female programmers. Today, a smartphone is billions of times more powerful than ENIAC.

cau_hoi: In 1844, the first telegram sent over the line from Washington to Baltimore by Samuel Morse contained what message?
giai_thich: The phrase is from the Bible, chosen by the daughter of a friend of Morse. Before the telegraph, news traveled quickly only by horse, train, or ship. After this invention, messages could travel across the United States in minutes. By 1866, telegraph cables were running under the Atlantic Ocean, connecting Europe with America.

cau_hoi: In 1854, at a fair in New York, Elisha Otis impressed the audience with which demonstration?
A: Flying in a hot air balloon over the city
C: Standing on an elevator and cutting the suspension cable, demonstrating that the safety brake would prevent the elevator from falling
D: Lighting an entire building with electricity
giai_thich: Previously, people were afraid to use elevators because the cable could break. Otis's safety brake consisted of notched teeth on either side of the elevator shaft; when the cable broke, a spring would pop out and hook onto the notches to hold the elevator. He stood on the elevator, ordered the cable to be cut, and said, "It's safe now, ladies and gentlemen!" Thanks to safe elevators, skyscrapers could be built.

cau_hoi: In 1902, engineer Willis Carrier invented the first modern air conditioner. What was its initial use?
B: Controlling humidity in a printing shop to prevent paper from warping
giai_thich: At the Sackett-Wilhelms printing shop (New York), humidity caused the paper to warp, misaligning the colored ink layers. Carrier's machine blew air through cold pipes, causing moisture to condense and reduce humidity, while also cooling the room. Later, air conditioning was installed in movie theaters, causing Americans to flock to summer films, and then into homes.

cau_hoi: In 1958, Momofuku Ando in Japan invented which food that is now consumed over 100 billion packets worldwide each year?
giai_thich: After World War II, Japan faced food shortages, and Ando wanted to create a cheap, tasty, and quick-to-cook noodle dish. In a shed behind his house, he experimented for a year and accidentally saw his wife frying tempura, which inspired him to fry the noodles to dry them and create small holes, allowing them to expand quickly when boiling water was added. In 1971, he created cup noodles. Vietnam is one of the countries that consumes the most instant noodles per capita.

cau_hoi: The arrangement of the QWERTY keyboard on computers originated from Christopher Sholes' typewriter in the 1870s. According to popular explanation, why are the letters arranged this way?
A: To make the letters look better when printed
B: To arrange them in alphabetical order
C: To type as quickly as possible
D: To prevent frequently used letter pairs from jamming when typing quickly
giai_thich: On old typewriters, each letter was attached to a metal arm. When typing quickly, two letters that were close together could jam. Sholes is believed to have separated commonly paired letters. Although mechanical typewriters have nearly disappeared, this arrangement remains because people are accustomed to it, a classic example of "habit hard to break" in technology.

cau_hoi: In 1804, Joseph Marie Jacquard invented the automatic loom capable of weaving complex patterns. Which idea from this loom later influenced computers?
C: Using punched cards to 'command' the machine
giai_thich: Each card had holes in different positions, determining which threads were lifted, so thousands of cards linked together would weave a picture. Babbage borrowed this idea for his analytical engine, and by the mid-20th century, punched cards were still used to input programs into computers. A woven portrait using the Jacquard loom required about 24,000 cards.

cau_hoi: In 1877, Thomas Edison successfully recorded speech for the first time using a phonograph. What did he read?
B: The nursery rhyme 'Mary had a little lamb'
giai_thich: Edison's phonograph had a needle attached to a diaphragm, etching grooves onto a tin foil wrapped around a rotating cylinder. When the needle ran back along the grooves, sound was produced. Even Edison's associates were astonished to hear his voice. In 2008, scientists found an older recording from France dating back to 1860, but that recording could not be played back at the time.

cau_hoi: British clockmaker John Harrison solved which problem with his ultra-accurate marine clock in the 18th century?
A: Determining a ship's longitude at sea
giai_thich: Sailors could easily measure latitude using the sun and stars, but to know longitude, they needed to know the time at the port of departure to compare with local time. Pendulum clocks did not keep accurate time on a rolling ship. Harrison took over 40 years to build his clock, and the H4, small like a large pocket watch, was only off by about 5 seconds after the trip to Jamaica in 1761-1762. Knowing the time discrepancy, sailors could calculate where the ship was.

cau_hoi: In 1608, which optician in the Netherlands submitted the first known patent application for the telescope?
giai_thich: According to legend, a child in Lippershey's shop played with two lenses and saw a distant church tower suddenly appear closer. His patent application was rejected because many others had also created similar devices. Hearing about this invention, Galileo made a better telescope in 1609 and pointed it at the sky, opening a new era of astronomy.

cau_hoi: Why does the oldest photograph by Niépce (circa 1826) of a rooftop show sunlight on both sides of the building?
A: The photo was stitched from two images
D: The exposure time lasted several hours, and the Sun moved from one side to the other
giai_thich: The light-sensitive materials of that time were very poor, so the camera had to keep the lens open from morning to afternoon, sometimes for several days. During this time, the Sun moved across the sky, illuminating both sides. Thus, the first photographs could only capture stationary scenes; to photograph a portrait, the model had to sit still for many minutes, sometimes with a headrest.

cau_hoi: How did the inventor Ctesibius in Alexandria (3rd century BC) improve the water clock to run more accurately?
B: Used a float to keep the water level flowing steadily
giai_thich: Simple water clocks ran unevenly because as the tank emptied, the water pressure decreased and the flow slowed. Ctesibius added a secondary tank with a float to maintain a stable water level, similar to the float in modern toilet tanks, ensuring a steady flow and making the clock more accurate than any other for nearly 1,800 years. He also invented a water pump used for firefighting and water-powered organs.

cau_hoi: The Islamic engineer al-Jazari (circa 1206) is famous for his "elephant clock." What is special about this clock?
B: Tells time with real elephant sounds
C: Runs on water, has moving figures of people and dragons that indicate the time, combining cultures from many regions
giai_thich: Inside the elephant is a water tank with a bowl that gradually sinks; when the bowl sinks completely, a mechanism pulls a ball to roll, a dragon spins, and the mahout rings a bell. Al-Jazari documented over 50 machines in his book "The Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices," including a water pump using a crankshaft. He is considered one of the pioneers of robotics.

cau_hoi: In 1088, the scholar Su Song in the Song dynasty of China built which famous structure?
A: The largest sailing ship in the world
B: A 12-meter tall water-powered astronomical clock tower
giai_thich: Su Song's clock tower had an astronomical globe rotating on top for star observation, figures that struck bells and drums to indicate the time, and a giant water wheel that turned steadily thanks to a braking mechanism. This mechanism is considered the ancestor of the escapement in mechanical clocks. Unfortunately, the tower was dismantled when the Jin army captured the capital in 1127, and no one knew how to reassemble it.

cau_hoi: In 1642, the 19-year-old Blaise Pascal invented the mechanical calculator "Pascaline" to help whom?
D: His father, a tax collector who had to do a lot of calculations
giai_thich: The Pascaline had gears numbered from 0 to 9; when one gear made a full turn, it pushed the adjacent gear forward one step, similar to a speedometer on a motorcycle. The machine could only directly add and subtract. Pascal made about 50 units but they did not sell well because they were too expensive and difficult to repair. The pressure unit pascal and a programming language are named after him.

cau_hoi: The German mathematician Gottfried Leibniz (17th century) developed which complete counting system, now the foundation of all computers?
C: Binary system (using only the two digits 0 and 1)
giai_thich: Leibniz realized that every number could be represented using only 0 and 1; for example, the number 5 is 101. He was fascinated to learn that the hexagrams in the Chinese I Ching, consisting of solid and broken lines, could be arranged similarly to the binary system. Computers use binary because electronic circuits can easily distinguish between two states: on and off. Leibniz also co-invented calculus with Newton.

cau_hoi: In 1807, how long did Robert Fulton's steamship Clermont take to travel on the Hudson River (USA) from New York to Albany?
giai_thich: The distance of about 240 km that sailing ships usually took about four days. Many mocked the ship as "Fulton's Folly," but it traveled steadily against the wind and current. Fulton was not the first to make a steamship, but he was the first to turn it into a profitable regular passenger service. Previously, he had also designed a submarine for Napoleon.

cau_hoi: In 1888, Scottish veterinarian John Boyd Dunlop created the first practical inflatable tire to help whom?
D: His son, to make his tricycle run smoother
giai_thich: Dunlop's son suffered from headaches because the tricycle with solid rubber tires bounced on the rocky road. He glued a rubber sheet into a tube, inflated it, and wrapped it around the wooden wheel. It turned out that Robert Thomson had patented the inflatable tire back in 1847 but it was forgotten. Inflatable tires made bicycles, and later cars, run much faster and smoother.

cau_hoi: The black and white barcode printed on goods was invented by Norman Woodland in 1948 while doing what?
B: Sitting on the beach, drawing dots and dashes of Morse code and then extending them into the sand
giai_thich: Woodland thought: if the dots and dashes of Morse code were extended into thin and thick lines, machines could read them quickly. His original design was circular like a target. It wasn't until 1974 that the UPC barcode was scanned for the first time in a supermarket in Ohio (USA). The first item scanned was a pack of chewing gum, which is now displayed in a museum.

cau_hoi: The QR code, created by engineer Masahiro Hara in 1994 in Japan, was inspired by what?
C: Black and white game pieces on a Go board
giai_thich: Hara worked for Denso Wave, which needed a type of code to help car factories track parts faster than barcodes. The QR code contains information in both horizontal and vertical directions, allowing it to store hundreds of times more data than a barcode, and the three squares in the corner help the reader recognize the code from any direction. The company decided not to charge royalties, so the QR code spread worldwide.

cau_hoi: In 1967, the world's first ATM was installed in London. What did users have to insert to withdraw money?
A: Special checks coated with a slight radioactive substance for the machine to recognize
giai_thich: Inventor John Shepherd-Barron said he came up with the idea for the machine while taking a bath after being late to the bank by a few minutes. He wanted a 6-digit PIN, but his wife said she could only remember 4 digits, so the 4-digit PIN became popular. The first machine only allowed withdrawals of up to 10 pounds at a time.

cau_hoi: In 1971, engineer Ray Tomlinson sent the first email between two computers and chose which symbol to separate the username from the computer name?
giai_thich: Tomlinson chose @ because it was available on the keyboard, almost no one used it in people's names, and in English, it means 'at'. The two computers were next to each other in the same room. He recalled that the content of the first email was probably a string of nonsense like 'QWERTYUIOP', and he doesn't remember exactly. In Vietnam, the @ symbol is often humorously referred to as 'a còng'.

cau_hoi: In 1968, engineer Douglas Engelbart demonstrated a computer control device with a wooden casing and two metal wheels. What did his team call it?
giai_thich: The device was called a 'mouse' because the cord at the back looked like a tail. In a 90-minute demonstration, later called 'The Mother of All Demos', Engelbart also introduced text editing on screens, hyperlinks, and video calling, things that would not become common for decades. He did not earn any royalties from the computer mouse.

cau_hoi: On October 29, 1969, the first message was sent over ARPANET, the precursor to the Internet, from UCLA to Stanford Institute. What happened?
A: The message was sent successfully on the first try
B: No one could read the message
C: The machine crashed after sending the two letters 'LO' (intending to type 'LOGIN')
D: The message was mistakenly sent to Russia
giai_thich: Student Charley Kline typed the letter L, then the letter O, and then the computer at Stanford crashed before receiving the letter G. Therefore, the first message of the Internet was 'LO', like the old English word 'lo' (look). About an hour later, the connection was restored, and the full LOGIN command was sent. Initially, ARPANET only connected four computers at four universities.

cau_hoi: The wireless technology 'Bluetooth' is named after whom?
B: Danish King Harald 'Bluetooth', who unified the Scandinavian tribes in the 10th century
giai_thich: In 1997, engineers from Intel, Ericsson, and Nokia temporarily named this project because the technology aimed to 'unify' different devices, just as King Harald unified the tribes. The temporary name was ultimately retained. The Bluetooth symbol is made up of the two runes H and B, the initials of the king's name, combined together.

cau_hoi: The first SMS message in the world, sent from a computer to a mobile phone on December 3, 1992, in the UK, contained what?
giai_thich: Engineer Neil Papworth typed the message on a computer and sent it to the phone of a Vodafone executive who was at a Christmas party. At that time, phones did not have keyboards to type reply messages. The SMS message was limited to 160 characters because engineer Friedhelm Hillebrand found that most postcards and short messages were within this length. In 2021, the first message was auctioned as an NFT.

cau_hoi: In 1975, engineer Steven Sasson at Kodak created the first digital camera. What was the quality of the first photo?
A: The photo was printed immediately on paper
C: Black and white, only about 0.01 megapixels, took 23 seconds to save to a cassette tape
D: Colors as sharp as today's phones
giai_thich: The camera weighed about 3.6 kg, about the size of a toaster. To view the photo, one had to plug the cassette into a separate device connected to a TV. Kodak's leaders were not very enthusiastic because the company made a lot of money from selling film. Ironically, digital cameras later contributed to Kodak's bankruptcy in 2012.

cau_hoi: In 1947, inventor Edwin Land announced the Polaroid camera that prints photos immediately after taking them. According to him, the idea came from whose question?
B: His 3-year-old daughter asking why she couldn't see the photo right away
giai_thich: During a vacation in 1943, Land's daughter asked why it took so long to see the photo her father had just taken. He spent several years creating a type of film that contained the chemicals needed for developing the photo, requiring only about 60 seconds to produce an image. The Polaroid camera became an icon for many generations. Land held about 535 patents in the U.S.

cau_hoi: In 1849, machinist Walter Hunt in New York invented the safety pin in just about 3 hours. What was his purpose?
B: To compete in an invention contest at school
C: To keep his coat from blowing away
D: To give to his wife for her birthday
giai_thich: Hunt bent a piece of wire into a coiled spring at one end and covered the sharp end with a cap, so the pin wouldn't poke anyone. He sold the patent for $400, paid off his debt, and still had money left over. The company that bought the patent made millions of dollars. Hunt also invented a type of sewing machine but did not apply for a patent because he feared it would put seamstresses out of work.

cau_hoi: In 1920, Earle Dickson, an employee of Johnson & Johnson, created the adhesive bandage (Band-Aid) to help whom?
A: His wife, who often cut her hands while cooking
giai_thich: Every time Josephine cut her hand, Dickson had to cut gauze and tape, which was difficult to do alone. He pre-attached small gauze pads to the tape and covered them with a layer of fabric to keep them clean, so his wife just had to cut a piece and stick it on. The company began selling the product in 1921; initially, it sold poorly until it was given away for free to Boy Scouts, which made it famous.

cau_hoi: In 1903, after seeing streetcar drivers in New York constantly sticking their heads out to wipe the windshield while it was snowing, who invented the windshield wiper?
giai_thich: Mary Anderson designed a rubber arm attached to the windshield, which the driver could pull from inside the car to wipe away snow and rain. Many companies refused to buy it because they thought it distracted drivers. The patent expired in 1920 before cars became popular, so she did not make money from her invention. By 1922, the windshield wiper had become standard equipment on Cadillac cars.

cau_hoi: In 1886, Josephine Cochrane in the United States invented the first usable water pressure dishwasher. What was her reason for creating it?
A: She wanted to go out more
C: Her maid often chipped her precious dishware
D: Her restaurant needed to wash quickly
giai_thich: Cochrane was a wealthy woman who often hosted parties. She designed metal wire racks that fit each plate and cup, placed in a rotating wheel, and hot soapy water was sprayed on them. Initially, the machine was sold to large hotels and restaurants. Her company later became part of KitchenAid.

cau_hoi: The world's first public railway using a steam locomotive, inaugurated in England in 1825, connected which two towns?
giai_thich: On September 27, 1825, the locomotive "Locomotion No. 1" designed by George Stephenson pulled a train carrying coal and hundreds of passengers at a speed of about 19 – 24 km/h. The original line primarily transported coal from the mines to the port. The distance between the two rails that Stephenson used, 1,435 mm, became the standard gauge for most of the world today.

cau_hoi: In 1938, Ruth Wakefield, owner of a restaurant in Massachusetts (USA), created which type of cookie by adding chocolate chips to cookie dough?
giai_thich: Wakefield was a trained baking expert, not a casual creator as some stories suggest; she intentionally added chopped chocolate pieces to create a new dish. She sold the recipe to Nestlé for a reported dollar plus a lifetime supply of chocolate. The recipe has been printed on Nestlé's chocolate packaging to this day.

cau_hoi: The famous slogan "You press the button, we do the rest" (1888) is associated with whose camera, allowing ordinary people to take photos?
giai_thich: Previously, photography required complex techniques and bulky equipment. Eastman's Kodak camera came pre-loaded with film that could take 100 pictures; after taking photos, users would send the entire camera back to the factory for developing and reloading. In 1900, the Brownie camera sold for just one dollar, allowing children to take photos as well. Eastman named it "Kodak" because he liked the letter K and wanted a short name that was easy to read in any language.

cau_hoi: In 1958, physicist William Higinbotham created "Tennis for Two" on an oscilloscope screen. What is this considered?
C: One of the first video games created for entertainment
giai_thich: Higinbotham worked at the Brookhaven National Laboratory (USA) and wanted something interesting for visitors on opening day. The game showed a ball bouncing over a net from a side view, with two players using hand-held controllers with knobs. Hundreds of people lined up to play. He did not apply for a patent, and the game was dismantled after two years.

cau_hoi: The puzzle game Tetris, one of the best-selling video games in history, was created in 1984 in which location?
B: The Soviet Union, by engineer Alexey Pajitnov
giai_thich: Pajitnov worked at the Soviet Academy of Sciences in Moscow. He was inspired by the pentomino puzzle but used blocks made up of 4 squares. The name "Tetris" is a combination of "tetra" (four) and "tennis," his favorite sport. Because the game was owned by the Soviet state, Pajitnov received almost no money until 1996.

cau_hoi: The first crossword puzzle was published by journalist Arthur Wynne in the New York World in 1913. What shape did it have?
B: Diamond shape, with no black squares
giai_thich: The first crossword, called "word-cross," was diamond-shaped with a blank space in the middle. Just a few years later, the name changed to "crossword" and black squares appeared to separate the words. By the 1920s, crosswords became a craze in the USA, to the extent that some libraries had to limit users from using dictionaries. The New York Times initially dismissed crosswords as "child's play" but began publishing them in 1942.

cau_hoi: Where does the name of the toy flying disc "Frisbee" come from?
A: A bakery named Frisbie, where students often threw empty pie tins to each other
C: The name of a bird species
giai_thich: College students in New England (USA) often threw back and forth the tin trays from Frisbie Pie Company and shouted "Frisbie!" to warn each other. In 1957, the toy company Wham-O bought Fred Morrison's plastic disc and renamed it "Frisbee." In 2010, Morrison passed away, and part of his ashes was molded into a Frisbee as per his wishes.

cau_hoi: The game Monopoly originated from a game created by Lizzie Magie in 1904 for what purpose?
A: To teach children how to get rich quickly
C: To show that land monopoly makes tenants poor and landlords rich
D: To train the memory of the elderly
giai_thich: Lizzie Magie's game "The Landlord's Game" had two sets of rules: one where everyone shared wealth when someone got rich, and another where the winner monopolized everything. She wanted players to see which set of rules was fairer. Many years later, Charles Darrow sold a version to Parker Brothers in 1935 and was considered the inventor, while Magie was nearly forgotten.

cau_hoi: Today's Wi-Fi technology is based on an important patent from scientists at CSIRO in which country?
giai_thich: In the early 1990s, John O'Sullivan's team at CSIRO solved the problem of radio signals bouncing off walls indoors, causing data to blur. Interestingly, their technique stemmed from a previous project: detecting signals from small black holes evaporating in space. CSIRO won many lawsuits and earned hundreds of millions of dollars in royalties.

cau_hoi: The CD, developed by Philips and Sony and first sold in 1982, was designed to hold a famous piece of music lasting approximately 74 minutes. What was it?
C: The national anthem of all countries
D: The entire album of the Beatles
giai_thich: According to Sony's story, vice president Norio Ohga, who was an opera singer, wanted the disc to hold the entire Ninth Symphony without having to flip it over. The longest recordings of the piece last about 74 minutes. Some researchers believe this is just a nice advertising story. The first music album produced on CD was Billy Joel's "52nd Street."

cau_hoi: The GPS system was originally only for the US military. What event in 1983 led President Reagan to announce that GPS would be made available for civilian use for free?
A: A ship sinking in the Arctic
C: An astronaut getting lost on the Moon
D: Korean Air Flight KAL 007 straying into Soviet airspace and being shot down
giai_thich: The Boeing 747 strayed off course due to navigation errors and was shot down by Soviet fighter jets, killing 269 people. To prevent a similar tragedy, the US decided to allow civilian aviation to use GPS. Initially, the signal for civilians was intentionally made less accurate; by 2000, this restriction was lifted, paving the way for today's phone maps.

cau_hoi: In 1971, Intel launched the first commercial microprocessor, the Intel 4004. What was it originally designed for?
A: A pocket calculator from the Japanese company Busicom
giai_thich: The tiny chip, the size of a fingernail, contained about 2,300 transistors, with computing power equivalent to the 27-ton ENIAC. Engineers Federico Faggin, Ted Hoff, Stanley Mazor, and Masatoshi Shima packed many functions into a single chip. Intel acquired the rights from Busicom, marking the beginning of the personal computer era. Today, a chip can contain tens of billions of transistors.

cau_hoi: In 1958, engineer Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments successfully created what, earning him the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2000?
giai_thich: Kilby was new to the company and did not get a summer vacation like everyone else; he stayed in the empty lab and devised a way to create multiple electronic components on a single piece of germanium semiconductor. A few months later, Robert Noyce at Fairchild independently created a more convenient silicon microchip for production. Noyce passed away in 1990, so he was not awarded the Nobel Prize, as the prize is not given posthumously.

cau_hoi: Hollywood star Hedy Lamarr and composer George Antheil were granted a patent in 1942 for which invention?
D: Frequency-hopping technique that makes torpedo control signals hard to jam
giai_thich: The idea was for the sender and receiver to continuously hop through 88 frequencies in a secret order, like the 88 keys of a piano, so the enemy would not know which frequency to jam. They were inspired by automatic pianos that ran on punched paper rolls. The US Navy did not use it immediately, but the same principle later contributed to Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and GPS.

cau_hoi: In 1947, Grace Hopper's computer science team affixed to their logbook a found object in the Harvard Mark II computer, contributing to the popularization of the term "bug" (computer error). What was that object?
A: A moth stuck in a relay
giai_thich: They noted: "The first case of a real bug found." The term "bug" to refer to machine errors had existed since Edison’s time, but this story made it famous in the computing industry, along with the term "debug." The log page with the moth is now preserved at the Smithsonian Institution. Grace Hopper also developed the first compiler and contributed to the creation of the COBOL programming language.

cau_hoi: The first traffic light in the world, installed in 1868 near the British Parliament building in London, was different from today's in what way?
B: Used gas lamps and a lever signal like railways, had to be operated manually by a policeman
C: Automatically changed colors using a computer
giai_thich: The light was designed by railway engineer John Peake Knight, using a lever during the day and red and green gas lamps at night. Less than a month later, the light leaked gas and exploded, injuring the policeman operating it. Electric traffic lights appeared in the US in 1914. In 1923, inventor Garrett Morgan was granted a patent for a signal that included a prepare-to-stop state, similar to today's yellow light.

cau_hoi: In 1959, engineer Nils Bohlin of Volvo (Sweden) invented the three-point seatbelt. What made Volvo's decision regarding this invention very special?
A: Volvo only used it for racing cars
B: Volvo sold the patent for a very high price
C: Volvo allowed all other car manufacturers to use the patent for free
D: Volvo kept it a secret for 50 years
giai_thich: The three-point seatbelt, which includes a strap across the chest and a strap across the hips, secures the person firmly and can be fastened with one hand. Volvo believed the invention was too important for human life to charge royalties. It is estimated that the three-point seatbelt has saved over a million lives worldwide. Before working for Volvo, Bohlin designed ejection seats for fighter jets.

cau_hoi: In 1901, British engineer Hubert Cecil Booth created the first motorized vacuum cleaner. What was its size?
A: As large as a horse-drawn carriage, parked outside with a long hose running through the window into the house
giai_thich: Booth saw a machine blowing dust off train seats, making dust fly everywhere, and thought of a way to suck up dust instead of blowing it. To test it, he placed a handkerchief on a seat and sucked with his mouth, nearly choking on the dust. His machine "Puffing Billy" ran on gasoline and was pulled by horses to each house. In 1902, it was used to clean the carpets at Westminster Abbey before the coronation of King Edward VII.

cau_hoi: Inventor Elias Howe recounted that he came up with the idea of placing the needle's eye at the tip of the needle, the key to creating the sewing machine in 1845 – 1846, thanks to what?
B: A dream about warriors with spears that had holes at the tips
D: Watching a spider spin its web
giai_thich: Hand sewing needles have the eye at the tail, but sewing machines need a needle that pierces the fabric and then pulls up, so the thread forms a loop with a second thread below. The dream story may be embellished, but the needle with an eye at the sharp end was indeed crucial. Howe had to litigate for many years to protect his patent, ultimately earning a large royalty from Isaac Singer and other companies.

cau_hoi: In 1793, Eli Whitney invented the cotton gin. What unfortunate consequence did this invention cause in the Southern United States?
A: Caused people to stop growing cotton
C: Cotton farming became very profitable, leading to an expansion of slavery
D: Increased the price of fabric tenfold
giai_thich: The cotton gin allowed one person to clean as much cotton as about 50 people could by hand. Instead of reducing labor, it made cotton farming highly profitable, causing plantation owners to expand their land and require more slaves to grow and pick cotton. The number of enslaved people in the U.S. increased from about 700,000 in 1790 to about 4 million by 1860. This is an example of how technology can have unintended social impacts.

cau_hoi: In 1829, the "Rocket" steam locomotive of father and son Stephenson won the Rainhill Trials in England. What was its maximum speed, which astonished people at the time?
giai_thich: The competition was held to select a locomotive for the Liverpool – Manchester railway. Rocket was the only locomotive to complete the challenges, thanks to its multi-tube boiler that produced steam quickly. Many people at the time feared that humans could not breathe at such high speeds. Today, Rocket is displayed at the Science Museum in London.

cau_hoi: In 1770, chemist Joseph Priestley named a material "rubber" because he discovered it could be used for what?
giai_thich: In English, "rub" means to rub or erase. Previously, people erased pencil marks using bread crumbs. Early rubber erasers were prone to damage and emitted odors when heated, until Goodyear vulcanized rubber in 1839. In 1858, Hymen Lipman was granted a patent for attaching an eraser to the end of a pencil. Today in England, erasers are still referred to as "rubber."

cau_hoi: Canned food was invented in the early 19th century, but how many years later did the specialized can opener come into existence?
giai_thich: The first tin cans were made from thick iron, very heavy, and soldiers had to open them with hammers, chisels, bayonets, or even gunfire. It wasn't until around 1858, when thinner metal cans were made, that Ezra Warner in the U.S. patented a can opener. The can opener with a rotating wheel as we know it today appeared in 1870. This is an interesting example of how one invention needs another to accompany it.

cau_hoi: Inventor Clarence Birdseye came up with the idea of quick-freezing food after observing what in Labrador (Canada)?
A: Polar bears burying food in the snow
C: Fish caught by Inuit freezing instantly in the cold wind, thawing still fresh
giai_thich: At temperatures around −40°C, fish freeze almost instantly, creating very small ice crystals that do not rupture cells, so when thawed, they remain fresh. Slow freezing creates large crystals, making food mushy and losing flavor. From the 1920s, Birdseye developed quick-freezing machines and sold packaged frozen foods, changing the way people eat worldwide.

cau_hoi: Tea bags are believed to have been invented around 1908 due to a misunderstanding by customers. What happened?
A: Someone dropped tea into a pocket
B: A child stuffed tea into a sock
C: Tea got wet in the rain while in a bag
D: Customers dipped the entire silk bag containing sample tea into boiling water instead of taking the tea out
giai_thich: New York merchant Thomas Sullivan sent tea samples to customers in small silk bags to save costs. Some customers thought they had to brew the whole bag and found it very convenient. Later, silk bags were replaced with muslin and then paper filters. Today, over 90% of tea in England is brewed using tea bags, although the English were initially very skeptical of this type of tea.

cau_hoi: In 1935, scientist Robert Watson-Watt was asked by the British government if it was possible to create a "death ray" using radio waves to kill people. What was the result of that question?
A: He said it was impossible, but suggested using radio waves to detect aircraft, leading to radar
giai_thich: Watson-Watt and assistant Arnold Wilkins calculated that it was impossible to generate enough energy to harm pilots, but radio waves bouncing off aircraft could be measured. They successfully tested in 1935 with a bomber aircraft. The radar chain "Chain Home" along the coast helped Britain detect German aircraft from afar during the Battle of Britain in 1940.

cau_hoi: Jet engines for aircraft were developed independently by two engineers in the 1930s. Who were they?
D: Frank Whittle (UK) and Hans von Ohain (Germany)
giai_thich: Whittle was granted a patent for the jet engine in 1930 at the age of 22, but did not receive much support from the British government. Von Ohain in Germany worked with Heinkel, and the German He 178 flew with a jet engine for the first time in 1939, nearly two years before the British aircraft. After the war, the two met, became friends, and received many awards together.

cau_hoi: In 1939, Russian-born inventor Igor Sikorsky tested the VS-300 in the U.S., paving the way for which type of vehicle to be mass-produced?
B: Helicopter with one main rotor and one tail rotor
giai_thich: Since the age of 12, Sikorsky dreamed of flying machines after reading Jules Verne's stories and seeing Leonardo da Vinci's sketches. The design with a large rotor and a small tail rotor to counteract the body’s rotation became the most popular helicopter type in the world. He stated that helicopters are excellent rescue vehicles because they can land anywhere.

cau_hoi: On May 6, 1937, the giant German airship Hindenburg caught fire while landing in New Jersey (USA). Why was this accident particularly dangerous?
A: The airship was filled with gunpowder
B: The airship was struck by lightning repeatedly
C: The airship was filled with highly flammable hydrogen gas
D: The airship was made of dry wood
giai_thich: The Hindenburg was about 245 meters long, nearly the same as the Titanic, carrying passengers across the Atlantic. It used hydrogen because the U.S., which had the most helium, restricted the export of this non-flammable gas. The fire consumed the airship in about half a minute, resulting in 36 fatalities. The scene was filmed and broadcast live, marking the end of the passenger airship era.

cau_hoi: In 1943, Jacques Cousteau and engineer Émile Gagnan invented which device that allowed people to swim freely underwater?
B: Diving regulator (aqualung) with a pressure valve
C: Copper diving suit with a large helmet
giai_thich: The most important component was the pressure valve, improved by Gagnan from a valve used for gas-powered cars, which automatically supplied air at the correct pressure of the surrounding water whenever the diver inhaled. Divers no longer needed a hose from the boat. Cousteau later made famous ocean films, such as "The Silent World," which won the Palme d'Or in 1956.

cau_hoi: In 1888, who created the film camera that is believed to have recorded the oldest existing film, "Roundhay Garden Scene" in England, lasting about 2 seconds?
giai_thich: Le Prince filmed his family walking in the garden in Leeds. In 1890, he boarded a train in France and mysteriously disappeared with his luggage, never to be found, before he could demonstrate his invention in the U.S. Thus, others like Edison and the Lumière brothers became more widely known as the fathers of cinema.

cau_hoi: In 1943, naval engineer Richard James accidentally dropped a testing spring and saw it "walk" down a shelf. What toy was invented from that?
giai_thich: James was trying to create a spring to stabilize equipment on a warship. The spring fell and did not stay still but flipped over, stepping down from the bookshelf to a stack of books and then to the floor. His wife, Betty, flipped through a dictionary and chose the word "slinky," meaning sleek and graceful. When launched in 1945, 400 units sold out in 90 minutes. The Slinky spring is also used by physicists to illustrate waves.

cau_hoi: Play-Doh, the familiar children's toy, was originally produced for what purpose?
C: A cleaner for soot on wallpaper
giai_thich: In the 1930s, homes heated with coal had walls stained with black soot, and this pliable substance was rolled on wallpaper to absorb dirt. As homes gradually switched to heating with oil, gas, and washable wallpaper, the product was about to be discarded. A kindergarten teacher used it for students to mold toys, and in 1956, Play-Doh was sold as a toy.

cau_hoi: In 1903, French chemist Édouard Bénédictus dropped a glass flask, which cracked but did not shatter. What invention did this discovery lead to?
B: Safety glass with multiple layers, used for car windshields
giai_thich: The glass flask once contained a solution of nitrocellulose, which dried to leave a thin plastic film inside that held the shards together. After reading about car accidents where people were injured by glass shards, Bénédictus made glass laminated with a layer of plastic in between. Today, car windshields are still made of laminated glass, which, when broken, only cracks like a spider web without sending sharp pieces flying out.

cau_hoi: In 1913, metallurgist Harry Brearley in Sheffield (England) invented stainless steel while searching for a better material for what?
giai_thich: Brearley experimented by adding chromium to steel. He found that steel samples containing about 12% chromium did not rust and were also not corroded by lemon juice or vinegar. Chromium creates a thin, invisible oxide layer on the surface that self-repairs when scratched. Sheffield, known for its knife-making, quickly produced stainless cutlery, and today stainless steel is found in every kitchen.

cau_hoi: In 1894, the Kellogg brothers in Michigan (USA) accidentally created which breakfast cereal when they forgot cooked wheat dough?
giai_thich: John Harvey Kellogg was a doctor running a sanatorium, wanting a light snack for patients. The two brothers forgot a batch of cooked wheat, and when rolled out, it became thin flakes, which they toasted until crispy. Later, they made it with corn. The younger brother, Will Keith Kellogg, added sugar for flavor and started his own company, becoming a world-famous cereal brand.

cau_hoi: The electric cotton candy machine, widely introduced at the 1904 World's Fair, was co-invented by someone in which profession, which sounds ironic?
giai_thich: In 1897, dentist William Morrison and candy maker John Wharton created a machine that spun hot melted sugar through small holes; the sugar strands met the air and cooled into fine threads like cotton. At the St. Louis Fair in 1904, they sold over 68,000 boxes of "fairy floss." Today, the name "cotton candy" was popularized by another dentist, Josef Lascaux.

cau_hoi: In 1823, chemist Johann Döbereiner invented a fire-starting device that was widely sold even before the safety match was invented. How did this device work?
B: Hydrogen gas sprayed onto a porous platinum piece, with platinum acting as a catalyst causing hydrogen to ignite
D: Using a magnifying glass to focus sunlight
giai_thich: In the "Döbereiner lamp", zinc reacts with acid to produce hydrogen. When the valve is opened, hydrogen sprays onto the platinum piece, and the platinum catalyzes the reaction with oxygen, heating up and igniting the hydrogen. This was one of the first practical applications of a catalyst, with around 20,000 units sold in the 1820s. Döbereiner is also famous for arranging elements into groups of three.

cau_hoi: In 1679, French physicist Denis Papin demonstrated the "steam digester", the ancestor of which modern kitchen appliance?
giai_thich: The pot with a tightly sealed lid retains steam inside, increasing pressure, allowing water to boil at temperatures above 100°C and softening even bones. To prevent the pot from exploding, Papin added a safety valve, an important invention later used in all steam boilers. He also observed steam pushing the lid up and thought of using steam to push a piston, a step towards the steam engine.

cau_hoi: In 1972, engineer Godfrey Hounsfield at EMI (UK) invented the computed tomography (CT) scanner. Where did EMI get most of the funding for this research?
A: Profits from selling records of The Beatles
D: Money from the British royal family
giai_thich: EMI was the record label for The Beatles, and many believe the band's great success helped the company fund new projects. The CT scanner takes X-rays from multiple angles and uses a computer to reconstruct images of cross-sections inside the body, showing the brain and organs much more clearly. Hounsfield and Allan Cormack received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1979.

cau_hoi: Australian doctor Graeme Clark, who developed the multi-channel cochlear implant (implanted in the first patient in 1978), recounted that he came up with the idea of threading electrodes into the cochlea by observing what?
A: Listening to the sound of ocean waves
B: Watching a worm burrow into the ground
D: Threading a blade of grass into a seashell on the beach
giai_thich: Clark's father was hearing impaired, so from a young age, he wanted to help the deaf hear. The major challenge was threading the electrode array into the coiled cochlea without causing damage. While on vacation at the beach, he noticed a soft blade of grass that became increasingly stiff from tip to root, which could be inserted deep into the shell. The cochlear implant converts sound into electrical signals that directly stimulate the auditory nerve, helping hundreds of thousands of people hear.

cau_hoi: In 1961, Czech chemist Otto Wichterle created the first soft contact lenses at home, using what special device?
A: His son's metal construction toy set, attached to a bicycle motor
giai_thich: Wichterle invented a soft, water-absorbing gel for the eyes, but his laboratory support was cut off by the authorities. During Christmas, he assembled a centrifuge from his son's Merkur toy set and cast the first four contact lenses on his kitchen table. Today, hundreds of millions of people worldwide wear soft contact lenses.

cau_hoi: During World War II, when Norway was occupied by Germany, what office supply did Norwegians wear on their clothes as a silent symbol of solidarity and resistance?
giai_thich: The paper clip "holds everything together", thus becoming a symbol of solidarity; wearing it could lead to arrest. Norwegians also believed that a Norwegian, Johan Vaaler, invented the paper clip, as he was granted a patent in Germany in 1899. In fact, the two-loop paper clip style (Gem style) became popular in England before that. In Sandvika, near the capital Oslo, there is a giant paper clip statue about 7 meters tall.

cau_hoi: In 2000, skydiver Adrian Nicholas successfully tested a parachute designed according to whose drawings from around 1485, made of cotton and wood?
giai_thich: The pyramid-shaped parachute weighed about 85 kg, and many experts believed it would spin or fall like a stone. Nicholas jumped from a balloon at an altitude of about 3,000 m in South Africa, and the parachute descended more gently than modern parachutes. For safety, he detached from it at about 600 m and opened a regular parachute. He said, "It took 500 years for someone to be brave enough to try" this design.

cau_hoi: In 1776, David Bushnell's submarine "Turtle" was used in the American War of Independence. How did it operate?
B: One person inside turned the hand-cranked propellers, containing enough air for about 30 minutes
giai_thich: The egg-shaped wooden vessel had hand-cranked propellers for lateral and vertical movement, along with a mine to attach to the enemy's hull. During an attack on a British ship in New York harbor, the pilot could not drill through the ship's hull and had to give up. Despite its failure, Turtle was the first submarine used in combat, and it used a luminous clock powered by bioluminescent fungi.

cau_hoi: Engineer Rudolf Diesel, the father of the diesel engine, demonstrated his engine running on what surprising fuel at the 1900 Paris World's Fair?
giai_thich: Diesel believed that his engine could help farmers and craftsmen run machines using vegetable oil they could grow. The diesel engine ignites fuel by compressing air to a very high temperature without needing a spark plug, thus achieving higher efficiency than gasoline engines. In 1913, he mysteriously disappeared from a ferry crossing the English Channel, and a few days later, his body was found at sea.

cau_hoi: In 1880, British inventors Joseph Swan and Thomas Edison both patented the incandescent light bulb. How did they resolve their dispute?
D: Cooperated to establish a joint company in England called "Ediswan"
giai_thich: Swan demonstrated the carbon filament bulb in England from late 1878 to 1879, nearly simultaneously with Edison in the US. Swan's house in Gateshead was the first home in the world to be lit by electric light bulbs, and the Savoy Theatre in London was the first public building. Instead of prolonged litigation, the two parties formed a joint company in 1883. History shows that many great inventions emerged almost simultaneously in various places.

cau_hoi: On February 14, 1876, the same day Alexander Graham Bell's lawyer filed a patent application for the telephone, another inventor also submitted a filing for a similar device. Who was that person?
giai_thich: Gray submitted a "patent caveat" just hours after Bell's application, according to many accounts. The dispute over who invented the telephone first lasted for decades with hundreds of lawsuits, and Bell won. This shows that many inventors were racing to create the telephone.

cau_hoi: The famous saying "Genius is 1% inspiration and 99% perspiration" is attributed to whom?
giai_thich: Edison was famous for working tirelessly and trying thousands of times. When asked about his failures in finding a filament material, he is said to have replied that he did not fail, but found thousands of ways that didn't work. His laboratory in Menlo Park, New Jersey, was one of the first "invention factories," where a team of engineers worked together; the press called him the "Wizard of Menlo Park."

cau_hoi: Why did the Wright brothers choose Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, as the site to test their airplane?
A: Because it had a large airport
B: Because there were many birds to observe
C: It had strong and steady winds to lift the plane, soft sand for safe landings, and few curious onlookers
D: Because it was closest to their home
giai_thich: The two brothers lived in Dayton, Ohio, hundreds of kilometers away from Kitty Hawk. They wrote to the U.S. Weather Bureau asking about places with strong and steady winds, and Kitty Hawk was recommended. The nearby Kill Devil Hills allowed them to test their gliders multiple times. Today, North Carolina's license plates read "First in Flight," while Ohio's say "Birthplace of Aviation."

cau_hoi: Brazilian pilot Alberto Santos-Dumont, who flew the first airplane in Europe in 1906, also contributed to popularizing which item?
giai_thich: Santos-Dumont complained that while flying, he couldn't take out his pocket watch to check the time. His friend, jeweler Louis Cartier, made him a wristwatch in 1904. At that time, wristwatches were mainly for women. In Brazil, many consider Santos-Dumont the true father of aviation because his 14-bis took off on its own with wheels, without needing a launch rail.

cau_hoi: In 1909, French pilot Louis Blériot achieved what feat with his monoplane?
B: First to fly across the English Channel from France to England
giai_thich: On July 25, 1909, Blériot flew for about 37 minutes from Calais to Dover, winning a £1,000 prize from the Daily Mail. He did not carry a compass and at times got lost in the clouds. The flight made the British realize that England was no longer a "protected island" by the sea, as airplanes could cross the channel in less than an hour.

cau_hoi: On Christmas Eve 1906, engineer Reginald Fessenden is said to have done what that astonished telegraph operators on ships when they heard through their headsets?
A: Broadcast radio voice and violin music, instead of just the beeping of Morse code
giai_thich: According to Fessenden, from the Brant Rock station in Massachusetts, he played "O Holy Night" on the violin and read a passage from the Bible. Previously, radio could only transmit intermittent signals of Morse code. He was a pioneer in transmitting sound via radio waves, the foundation of radio broadcasting. Some historians still question the details of this broadcast.

cau_hoi: Philo Farnsworth, one of the fathers of electronic television, conceived of the idea of scanning images line by line when he was just 14 years old, thanks to observing what?
A: The rows of bricks on the pavement
B: The lines of text in books
C: The stripes on a zebra's back
D: The parallel rows of soil when plowing potato fields
giai_thich: While plowing fields on a farm in Idaho, young Farnsworth looked at the straight rows of soil and thought that images could be "scanned" line by line using an electron beam, then reconstructed at the receiver. In 1927, at the age of 21, he successfully transmitted the first image, a straight line. He had to litigate with RCA for many years to protect his patent.

cau_hoi: Engineer Ralph Baer, who created the "Brown Box" in 1967-1968, is considered the father of which type of product?
C: Home video game consoles that connect to TVs
giai_thich: Baer thought that millions of televisions in households could be used for something other than watching programs. His "Brown Box" featured simple ping-pong and volleyball games and was sold under the name Magnavox Odyssey in 1972, the first home video game console. Baer was a German Jew who fled to America in 1938 at the age of 16.

cau_hoi: The Japanese company Nintendo, famous for Mario and Pokémon, was founded in 1889 to produce what?
giai_thich: Fusajiro Yamauchi opened a shop making Hanafuda cards in Kyoto. Before transitioning to video games, Nintendo experimented with various businesses such as taxi services, hotels, and instant noodles. The name "Nintendo" is often understood to mean "leave luck to heaven." Today, the company still sells Hanafuda cards.

cau_hoi: In 1979, Sony launched the portable cassette player Walkman. According to the famous story, who was the person who wanted this device?
A: Co-founder Masaru Ibuka, who wanted to listen to music on long flights
giai_thich: Ibuka asked engineers to make a compact music player, and they eventually removed the recording and speaker parts of the tape recorder, keeping only the music playback through headphones. Many in the company were skeptical because the device couldn't record. However, the Walkman sold about 200 million units, changing the way people listened to music, allowing them to take their music anywhere.

cau_hoi: In 2007, when introducing the first iPhone, Steve Jobs said he was about to introduce "three revolutionary products." What were they actually?
C: A TV, a car, and a watch
D: A single device that combines a music player, a phone, and an Internet access device
giai_thich: Jobs repeatedly stated "one iPod, one phone, one Internet communication device" until the audience realized it was just one device. The iPhone had no physical keyboard, only a multi-touch screen. Although smartphones existed before, the iPhone changed how phones were designed and used.

cau_hoi: The first video uploaded to YouTube on April 23, 2005, titled "Me at the zoo," is about what?
A: A co-founder standing in front of the elephant enclosure, talking about their long trunks for 19 seconds
giai_thich: Jawed Karim, one of the three founders of YouTube, filmed the video at the San Diego Zoo. He said, "The interesting thing about these animals is that they have really, really, really long trunks." The video is still on YouTube with hundreds of millions of views. Just over a year later, Google bought YouTube for $1.65 billion.

cau_hoi: In 1965, Gordon Moore, co-founder of Intel, made which famous prediction, now known as "Moore's Law"?
A: The Internet will cover the world by 1980
B: Computers will be able to speak by 1970
C: The number of transistors on a chip will double approximately every two years
D: The price of computers will double every year
giai_thich: Initially, Moore predicted doubling every year, but in 1975 he revised it to about two years. This is not a natural law but a trend, yet it has been strangely accurate for over 50 years and has become a "goal" for the entire industry. As a result, computers have become smaller, more powerful, and cheaper. Today, transistors are as small as a few dozen atoms, so the growth rate has slowed.

cau_hoi: In 1976, where did Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak start assembling the first Apple I computers, according to the famous story?
giai_thich: Wozniak designed the machine, while Jobs handled sales. To raise money, Jobs sold his Volkswagen bus and Wozniak sold his HP pocket calculator. The Apple I was sold for $666.66, just a circuit board, and buyers had to assemble the case, keyboard, and monitor themselves. Wozniak later said the garage was just a promotional story; most of the work actually took place elsewhere.

cau_hoi: In 1926, Robert Goddard successfully launched the first liquid-fueled rocket in the U.S. In 1920, the New York Times mocked him for what, and then had to publish a correction in 1969?
A: Claiming rockets could not be made of metal
B: Claiming rockets could not fly in a vacuum because there was no air to push against
C: Claiming he did not know math
giai_thich: Goddard's first rocket flew for only about 2.5 seconds, reaching an altitude of about 12.5 meters, and fell into a cabbage field owned by his aunt. The 1920 editorial claimed Goddard lacked "knowledge taught in high school." On July 17, 1969, as Apollo 11 was heading to the Moon, the paper published a correction stating that rockets could operate in a vacuum, "and we regret the error."

cau_hoi: Russian scientist Konstantin Tsiolkovsky, a pioneer of space travel, is famous for which quote?
D: "Earth is the cradle of humanity, but mankind cannot stay in the cradle forever"
giai_thich: Tsiolkovsky was nearly completely deaf from the age of 10 due to scarlet fever, taught himself in libraries, and became a teacher in a small town. In 1903, he published the "rocket equation" stating that the speed achieved by a rocket depends on the exhaust velocity and fuel ratio, and proposed multi-stage rockets. He also dreamed of space elevators and space stations, long before airplanes existed.

cau_hoi: On April 12, 1961, when the rocket launched Vostok 1, what famous phrase did Yuri Gagarin say?
giai_thich: Gagarin orbited the Earth for about 108 minutes, becoming the first person to travel into space. He parachuted out of the capsule at an altitude of about 7 km and landed in a field, astonishing a farmer and her granddaughter when they saw a man in an orange suit falling from the sky. He described the Earth from space as having "a beautiful blue halo."

cau_hoi: The term "robot" first appeared in the play "R.U.R." in 1920 by Czech writer Karel Čapek. According to Čapek, who suggested this term to him?
giai_thich: Initially, Karel intended to call the robots "labori" (from the Latin word for "labor"), but his brother Josef suggested the term "robot," derived from "robota" meaning forced labor. In the play, the robots are created to work for humans, but eventually revolt. Within a few years, the term "robot" was used worldwide.

cau_hoi: "Black boxes" record flight data and cockpit sounds, invented by Australian scientist David Warren in the 1950s. What color are they actually?
giai_thich: In 1953, while investigating the mysterious Comet plane crashes, Warren thought that if there were a device to record sounds in the cockpit, it would be easier to find the cause. Initially, many pilots opposed it because they did not want to be "eavesdropped on." The box is painted bright orange to be easily found among the wreckage, withstand extreme impacts, fire, and deep seawater. The name "black box" likely comes from the way mysterious electronic devices are referred to.

cau_hoi: In 2002, the U.S. House of Representatives passed a resolution recognizing an Italian immigrant inventor who had created a voice transmission device years before Bell but was too poor to maintain the patent. Who was he?
giai_thich: Meucci designed the "telettrofono" around the 1850s – 1860s to talk to his sick wife in another room. In 1871, he filed a patent application but only had enough money to extend it until 1874. The 2002 resolution recognized his contributions, although historians still debate the actual extent of his influence on Bell's telephone.

cau_hoi: In 1943, the U.S. Supreme Court issued a ruling related to radio patents. What did this ruling do?
A: Awarded the Nobel Prize to Tesla
C: Revoked Marconi's important patent, recognizing earlier patents by Nikola Tesla and others
D: Recognized Marconi as the sole inventor of the radio
giai_thich: The ruling came a few months after Tesla died in poverty in a New York hotel room. The lawsuit was related to the Marconi company's claim against the U.S. government for royalties. Nevertheless, Marconi is still remembered as the one who turned radio into a practical technology, and he received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1909. Radio is actually the result of many scientists.

cau_hoi: A Nintendo Game Boy handheld gaming console was singed in a bombing during the Gulf War (1991). What is it famous for?
A: It still ran Tetris and was displayed at the Nintendo store in New York
B: It was sold for 1 million dollars
giai_thich: The console belonged to a soldier and was heavily damaged when the barracks were bombed, with the plastic casing melted and blistered. However, when a new battery was installed, the screen still lit up. The Game Boy, released in 1989, is famous for its durability and long battery life due to its monochrome green screen. The design was based on the philosophy of engineer Gunpei Yokoi: using mature old technology in a creative way.

cau_hoi: In 1999, designer Shigetaka Kurita at NTT Docomo (Japan) created the first widely used emoji set. How many emojis were in this set?
giai_thich: Kurita wanted mobile phone users to convey emotions in short messages, inspired by weather symbols and manga comics. Each emoji was only 12×12 pixels. The term "emoji" is a combination of the Japanese "e" (picture) and "moji" (character), unrelated to the English word "emotion." In 2016, the original emoji set was included in the collection of the Museum of Modern Art in New York (MoMA).

cau_hoi: In 1982, computer scientist Scott Fahlman at Carnegie Mellon University proposed using which symbol to mark joke messages on electronic bulletin boards?
giai_thich: On the university's electronic bulletin board, jokes were often misunderstood as serious by readers. Fahlman proposed using :-) for light-hearted messages and :-( for serious ones, tilting one's head to the left to see the face. The idea spread quickly across computer networks. The original record of this message was lost and was only recovered in 2002 from old backup tapes.

cau_hoi: In 2007, who proposed using the # (hashtag) symbol to group posts on the same topic on the social network Twitter?
giai_thich: Messina wrote: "What do you think about using # (hashtag) for groups, like #barcamp?" Initially, Twitter thought this idea was too "technical." However, during a wildfire in California at the end of 2007, people used #sandiegofire to update news, and the hashtag gradually became popular. Messina did not patent this idea.

cau_hoi: Computer scientist Luis von Ahn created reCAPTCHA (around 2007), a type of box requiring users to type distorted letters. Besides blocking automated computers, what else does it help with?
A: Digitizing old books and newspapers by having users decipher unreadable letters
B: Counting the number of Internet users
giai_thich: Every day, hundreds of millions of people type CAPTCHA, each time taking a few seconds. Von Ahn thought of leveraging that effort: displaying a known word for verification and a hard-to-read word taken from old books. Thanks to millions of people, the archive of The New York Times from 1851 was digitized. He later founded the language learning app Duolingo.

cau_hoi: In 1971, the program "Creeper" spread between computers on the ARPANET, considered one of the first "computer worms." What message did it display?
C: "I am Creeper: catch me if you can!"
giai_thich: Creeper was created by Bob Thomas as a harmless experiment that did not destroy data. It moved from one machine to another and displayed a teasing message.
