Soon after, Ray Tomlinson (the inventor of email) wrote the program "Reaper" to chase and delete Creeper, considered the first antivirus software.

cau_hoi: "The Y2K Incident" that the whole world worried about before the year 2000 originated from what?
A: Computers would run out of memory in the year 2000
B: Many computer programs only stored the year in two digits, so the year 2000 could be misinterpreted as 1900
giai_thich: At a time when computer memory was still expensive, programmers saved space by writing "99" instead of "1999." When the year 2000 came, "00" could be interpreted by machines as 1900, causing errors in calculations at banks, airports, and power plants. Countries spent hundreds of billions of dollars to fix software. As a result, January 1, 2000, passed almost peacefully, leading some to mistakenly believe it was an overreaction.

cau_hoi: In 1975, Bill Gates and Paul Allen wrote the first software for Microsoft for which computer?
giai_thich: Seeing the Altair 8800 on the cover of Popular Electronics magazine, the two called the manufacturer and claimed they had a BASIC interpreter ready for the machine, even though they hadn't written a line yet. They worked day and night for about two months without having a real Altair machine to test. The first time it ran on the actual machine, the program worked immediately. Gates was only 19 years old at the time.

cau_hoi: In 1991, 21-year-old Finnish student Linus Torvalds began writing the kernel of which operating system as a "hobby," now running on most servers and Android phones?
giai_thich: Torvalds wrote on a forum: "I'm doing an operating system (free, just a hobby, won't be big and professional)." He allowed everyone to view and modify the source code, so thousands of programmers around the world joined in development. Today, Linux runs on all 500 of the world's most powerful supercomputers. Its mascot is the penguin Tux.

cau_hoi: The programming language Python, created by Guido van Rossum from around 1989 to 1991, is named after what?
A: The British television comedy show "Monty Python's Flying Circus"
giai_thich: Van Rossum started writing Python during the Christmas holiday as a hobby project in the Netherlands and chose a short, unique, slightly mysterious name from his favorite comedy show. Python was designed to be easy to read, resembling English, and is now the most popular language for teaching programming and artificial intelligence. The python image was only added to the logo later.

cau_hoi: In 1991, computer scientists at the University of Cambridge (UK) pointed a camera at the coffee pot in the break room. Why is this camera famous?
D: Considered the first webcam, it could later be viewed over the Internet from around the world
giai_thich: People working on different floors didn't want to walk to the break room only to find the pot empty. They attached a camera that took pictures of the pot several times a minute, viewable on the internal network. In 1993, the images were put on the web, and millions of people around the world logged in to see a coffee pot. In 2001, the pot was auctioned on eBay for about £3,350.

cau_hoi: In 1997, IBM's supercomputer Deep Blue achieved what for the first time in history?
B: Defeated world chess champion Garry Kasparov in a multi-game match with standard time controls
D: Drove autonomously across the United States
giai_thich: The rematch in New York consisted of 6 games, with Deep Blue winning 3.5 – 2.5. The machine could calculate about 200 million moves per second. A year earlier, Kasparov had defeated the previous version of the machine. Kasparov suspected human intervention due to a move that seemed too "human-like", but later many experts suggested that the move could have been a software error.

cau_hoi: In 2016, Google's DeepMind program AlphaGo defeated Go player Lee Sedol (South Korea) 4 – 1. Which move in the second game astonished the Go community?
A: The first move in the center of the board
C: "Move 37", a move that human experts almost never choose
giai_thich: Commentators initially thought it was a mistake, as AlphaGo calculated the probability of a human player choosing this move to be only about 1 in 10,000. However, it turned out to be the key move that helped the machine win. Go has more possible board positions than there are atoms in the observable universe, so many believed that computers would need decades to defeat humans.

cau_hoi: The ChatGPT chatbot launched at the end of November 2022 set what record for user growth speed?
A: Reached about 100 million users in just about two months
B: Had no users in its first year
D: Could only be used in one country
giai_thich: According to estimates published in early 2023, this is the fastest-growing consumer application up to that point; the social network TikTok took about nine months and Instagram about two and a half years to reach similar milestones. This event marked the wave of generative artificial intelligence, capable of writing text, answering questions, and coding. These chatbots are very useful but can still provide incorrect information, so users need to verify it.

cau_hoi: In 1950, Alan Turing proposed a test now known as the "Turing Test" to answer what question?
C: Whether a machine can converse like a human to the extent that people cannot distinguish it
giai_thich: In the paper "Computing Machinery and Intelligence", Turing proposed the "imitation game": a person converses in writing with a human and a machine without seeing them; if they cannot guess which is the machine, the machine can be considered to "think". He predicted that by around 2000, machines would deceive many people within minutes. This test is still widely discussed when talking about artificial intelligence.

cau_hoi: In 1942, science fiction writer Isaac Asimov introduced the "Three Laws of Robotics". What does the first law state?
B: Robots must always be fully charged
D: Robots must not harm humans, or allow humans to come to harm through inaction
giai_thich: The three laws are: not to harm humans; to obey human orders unless it conflicts with the first law; to protect themselves unless it conflicts with the first two laws. Asimov used them to write stories about dilemmas when the laws conflict. Although they are just fiction, they are still referenced in discussions about the ethics of robots and artificial intelligence.

cau_hoi: The humanoid robot ASIMO from Honda, launched in 2000, is famous for what ability?
B: Walking, running, and climbing stairs on two legs quite naturally
giai_thich: Walking on two legs is very difficult for robots, as they must constantly maintain balance like humans. Honda researched since 1986 to create ASIMO. Later versions can run about 9 km/h, pour water, play soccer, and recognize faces. ASIMO has met many heads of state and "retired" in 2022. The robot's name is reminiscent of writer Asimov, although Honda states it is an acronym for an English phrase.

cau_hoi: Engineer Wernher von Braun led the design of which rocket that took Apollo astronauts to the Moon?
giai_thich: Saturn V is about 111 m tall, taller than the Statue of Liberty, and was the most powerful rocket to successfully fly at that time. In 13 launches, it did not lose any astronauts. Von Braun previously built the V-2 rocket for the Nazis, a weapon produced using forced labor, a controversial part of his past.

cau_hoi: Engineer Sergei Korolev, who was behind Sputnik and Gagarin's flight, had what special aspect about his identity while alive?
D: His name was kept secret, referred to only as "Chief Designer"
giai_thich: The Soviet Union feared he would be assassinated or kidnapped by adversaries, so they concealed his name. Previously, in 1938, Korolev had been wrongfully imprisoned during Stalin's purges and sent to a labor camp in the Kolyma gold mines, losing many teeth due to illness. Only after his death in 1966 did the world learn the name of the person behind the Soviet space successes.

cau_hoi: What was the purpose of the "memory foam" developed in 1966 for use in pillows and mattresses?
A: To make airplane seat cushions for NASA to reduce shock
giai_thich: Engineer Charles Yost, working on a NASA project, created foam that molds to the shape of the body when compressed and slowly returns to its original shape. It helps distribute impact forces more evenly. Many other everyday products also originated from space research, such as camera sensors in phones and scratch-resistant lens coatings.

cau_hoi: What task was Professor Tran Dai Nghia (1913 – 1997), one of Vietnam's great scientists, assigned by President Ho Chi Minh when he returned to the country in 1946?
B: In charge of researching and manufacturing weapons for the resistance against the French
giai_thich: His real name was Pham Quang Le, and he studied and worked as an engineer in France. In 1946, he left a high-paying job to follow Uncle Ho back to the country, where he was given the new name Tran Dai Nghia. Despite the scarcity of resources, he and his colleagues developed bazookas and recoil-less guns to combat tanks and bunkers. He was one of the first to be honored as a Labor Hero.

cau_hoi: What notable contribution did Professor Luong Dinh Cua (1920 – 1975), a famous agronomist in Vietnam, make?
C: Crossbreeding many high-yield rice varieties and new crops, contributing to increased food production
giai_thich: He studied agriculture in Japan, earned a doctorate at Kyushu University, and in 1952 returned home with his family to participate in the resistance, later moving to the North. He and his colleagues crossbred many high-yield short-duration rice varieties, as well as watermelon, papaya, and many other crops. He was posthumously awarded the Ho Chi Minh Prize for Science and Technology in 1996.

cau_hoi: The name of the company Google, founded in 1998, comes from the word "googol." What is a googol?
giai_thich: The term "googol" was coined by 9-year-old Milton Sirotta, the nephew of mathematician Edward Kasner, in 1920 when asked what to call a huge number. Larry Page and Sergey Brin chose this name to represent their goal of organizing the vast amount of information on the web, although there is a story that they misspelled it as "Google." A googol is much larger than the number of atoms in the observable universe.

cau_hoi: In 1843, Scottish inventor Alexander Bain was granted a patent for a device that transmitted images over wires, the ancestor of which machine?
giai_thich: Many are surprised to learn that the fax machine was invented over 30 years before the telephone. Bain's device used two synchronized pendulums at each end of the wire, one scanning over raised metal letters, while the other printed on chemically treated paper that changed color when electric current passed through. Bain was a clockmaker and also invented the electric clock. It wasn't until the 1980s and 1990s that fax machines became common in offices.

cau_hoi: In addition to traffic signals, what else is American inventor Garrett Morgan, of African descent, famous for in 1916?
A: Using his invented gas mask to rescue workers trapped in a toxic gas-filled tunnel under Lake Erie
giai_thich: An explosion in a tunnel under Lake Erie (Cleveland) left many workers trapped in smoke and toxic gas. Morgan and his brother donned his "safety helmet," a hooded mask with a tube supplying clean air from near the ground, to descend into the tunnel to rescue people. Due to the racial discrimination of the time, many customers were reluctant to buy products from a Black man, so he sometimes had to hire white people to demonstrate.

cau_hoi: The Diners Club payment card (1950), considered the first multipurpose credit card, was created after what incident involving businessman Frank McNamara?
A: He ran out of money while traveling abroad
B: He forgot his wallet while dining at a restaurant and couldn't pay the bill
D: He wanted to buy a car
giai_thich: According to the company's story, McNamara had to call his wife to bring money to pay. A few months later, he returned to the restaurant and paid with a cardboard card, an event known as the "First Dinner." Initially, the card was only accepted at about 27 restaurants in New York. The plastic card with a magnetic stripe appeared later, and today it is a chip card.

cau_hoi: The online encyclopedia Wikipedia, launched on January 15, 2001, differs from traditional encyclopedias in what way?
A: You have to pay a fee to read it
C: It is only available in English
D: Almost anyone can write and edit articles, free for everyone
giai_thich: Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger created Wikipedia as a side project to supplement Nupedia, an online encyclopedia written by experts but progressing very slowly. The name is a portmanteau of "wiki" (Hawaiian for "quick") and "encyclopedia." Today, Wikipedia has millions of articles in over 300 languages, including Vietnamese. Since anyone can edit, readers should check the cited sources.

cau_hoi: Colossus, the world's first programmable electronic digital computer (1944), was built by engineer Tommy Flowers in England to do what?
C: Decrypt the encrypted messages of the German High Command encoded by the Lorenz machine
giai_thich: Colossus used about 1,600 – 2,400 vacuum tubes and read punched paper tape at a speed of 5,000 characters per second. Thanks to it, the Allies were able to read information before the Normandy landings. After the war, Prime Minister Churchill ordered the destruction of nearly all the machines, and the existence of Colossus remained a secret until the 1970s, so for many years ENIAC was considered the first electronic computer.

cau_hoi: In 1941, which German engineer created the Z3, considered the world's first fully automatic, programmable computer that used telephone relays?
giai_thich: Zuse began building computers in his parents' living room in Berlin because he was bored with repetitive calculations in his work as an aircraft engineer. The Z3 used a binary system and read programs from punched film. The machine was destroyed in a bombing raid in 1943. Zuse also designed Plankalkül, one of the first high-level programming languages.

cau_hoi: In 1957, eight young scientists left William Shockley's company to establish Fairchild Semiconductor, marking the beginning of Silicon Valley. What nickname did Shockley give them?
giai_thich: Shockley, co-inventor of the transistor, was very skilled in science but managed his staff with strictness and suspicion. The eight, including Robert Noyce and Gordon Moore, left to start their own company. From Fairchild, former employees went on to establish dozens of other companies like Intel and AMD, humorously referred to as "the children of Fairchild." This is how the plum-growing region near San Francisco became the world's technology hub.

cau_hoi: What was the first domain name ".com" registered on the Internet on March 15, 1985?
giai_thich: Symbolics was a small computer company in Massachusetts (USA) that specialized in producing computers for artificial intelligence research. In 1985, there were fewer than 10 .com domain names registered for the entire year, while today there are hundreds of millions. The Symbolics company went bankrupt, but the domain still exists as a historical site. In 2009, it was sold to an investor.

cau_hoi: In 1978, DEC employee Gary Thuerk sent a mass advertising message to about 400 ARPANET users. What is this message considered?
C: The first love letter sent online
giai_thich: Thuerk invited users to see a demonstration of the company's new computer. Many recipients were very angry because the message took up space in their inbox, but the company sold a few more machines. The term "spam" comes from a Monty Python sketch, where the canned meat Spam is mentioned so often that it drowns out all conversation.

cau_hoi: "Brain" (1986), one of the first personal computer viruses, was created by two brothers in Lahore (Pakistan) for what purpose, according to them?
A: To combat the unauthorized copying of their medical software
giai_thich: Basit and Amjad Farooq Alvi wrote a virus that spread via bootable floppy disks. Notably, they included their name, address, and store phone number in the virus code, along with a reminder to contact them for "repairs." The virus spread worldwide via floppy disks, and they received many calls from all over. In 2011, a security researcher visited Lahore and met the two brothers at the address listed in the virus.

cau_hoi: Before electronic computers, what did the term "computer" originally refer to in English?
A: People who performed calculations by hand
giai_thich: Since the 17th century, "computer" referred to a profession: people who specialized in calculating numerical tables for astronomy, navigation, and artillery. During World War II and the early space program, many women worked as "human computers," like the group of female mathematicians at NASA in the film "Hidden Figures." When electronic computers emerged, they were called "automatic computers" to distinguish them from humans, and gradually the term "computer" became reserved for machines.

cau_hoi: The book "Jikji" (1377), printed in Korea, holds what record recognized by UNESCO?
B: The oldest existing book printed with movable metal type
D: The thickest book in the world
giai_thich: Jikji is a collection of Buddhist texts, printed at Heungdeok Temple about 78 years before the Gutenberg Bible. Only the second volume is preserved, and it is located at the National Library of France in Paris, brought back from the 19th century, leading to years of debate between Korea and France. In 2001, Jikji was included in UNESCO's Memory of the World Register.

cau_hoi: Around 875, inventor Abbas ibn Firnas in Córdoba (Al-Andalus) is said to have done what bold act?
B: Climbed the highest mountain in Europe
C: Wore feathered wings and glided down from above, then landed injured
giai_thich: According to records, he donned a frame covered in silk and bird feathers, jumped from a hill, and glided for a distance. Upon landing, he injured his back, and it is believed he forgot to make a "tail" for balance like a bird. Ibn Firnas is also credited with inventing a water clock and a method for cutting crystal. An airport in Iraq and a crater on the Moon are named after him.

cau_hoi: British engineer George Cayley, considered the "father of aviation," allowed whom to test fly his glider in 1853?
D: His coachman, who is said to have quit immediately afterward
giai_thich: Cayley was the first to separate the forces acting on an aircraft: lift, thrust, drag, and weight, and proposed fixed-wing aircraft instead of flapping wings like birds. His manned glider flew over a small valley in Brompton Dale. According to legend, the coachman was so frightened that he said he was hired to drive horses, not to fly.

cau_hoi: German engineer Otto Lilienthal, the "king of gliders" with about 2,000 gliding flights, influenced the Wright brothers in what way?
A: He was a competitor who defeated them
B: He taught them how to fly
D: His writings and photographs of him gliding inspired and provided data for them
giai_thich: Lilienthal made thousands of gliding flights from hills near Berlin, and photographs of him soaring in the sky convinced the world that humans could fly. In 1896, he fell when his glider encountered a gust of wind and died. His last words are said to be "There must be sacrifice." News of his death spurred the Wright brothers to begin serious research into flight.

cau_hoi: In August 1783, the first unmanned hydrogen balloon of physicist Jacques Charles flew and landed in the village of Gonesse near Paris. How did the villagers react?
A: They panicked, thinking it was a monster and attacked it with pitchforks and knives
D: They invited it into the church
giai_thich: The silk balloon filled with hydrogen flew for about 45 minutes, covering approximately 21 km. When it landed, the villagers had never seen anything like it, thinking it was a monster from the sky and tore it apart. After this event, the French government had to issue a statement explaining to the public that the balloon was harmless. Four months later, Charles flew up in a hydrogen balloon himself.

cau_hoi: In 1769, French military engineer Nicolas-Joseph Cugnot built the first steam-powered vehicle to tow artillery. What is this vehicle believed to have caused?
B: One of the first motor vehicle accidents when it crashed into a wall
D: The first vehicle to carry the King of France
giai_thich: The heavy three-wheeled vehicle could only run about 4 km/h and had to stop every 15 minutes to build up steam. Due to the heavy boiler at the front, the vehicle was difficult to steer and, according to a story, crashed into a wall. Although unsuccessful, Cugnot's vehicle is considered the first self-propelled motor vehicle. A replica of the vehicle is currently on display in Paris.

cau_hoi: "The Red Flag Act" of 1865 in England imposed what strange requirement on motor vehicles on the road?
A: They could only operate at night
B: Vehicles had to be painted red
C: A pedestrian had to walk in front waving a red flag to warn others, and vehicles could only travel at about 6 km/h in the city
D: They had to be pulled by a horse
giai_thich: The act aimed to protect pedestrians and horses from noisy, heavy steam vehicles, but it also slowed the development of automobiles in England. The speed limit was about 4 miles per hour in rural areas and 2 miles per hour in cities. In 1896, the law was repealed, and motorists organized a trip from London to Brighton to celebrate, an event that is still held annually.

cau_hoi: In 1913, Henry Ford introduced the moving assembly line in the Model T factory. How did the time to assemble a car change?
A: Reduced from about 12 hours to about 1 hour and 30 minutes
giai_thich: Instead of workers moving around the car, the car was slowly pulled through each station, with each worker doing just one task. The idea was inspired by slaughterhouses in Chicago. Cars became much cheaper, allowing even workers to buy them. Ford said customers could choose "any color, as long as it's black," because black paint dried the fastest, fitting the speed of the assembly line.

cau_hoi: Where does the car brand name "Mercedes" originate from?
A: The name of a city in Spain
B: The name of Karl Benz's wife
C: The name of a Roman goddess
D: The name of the daughter of businessman Emil Jellinek, who ordered cars from Daimler
giai_thich: Jellinek was a wealthy businessman and racing enthusiast. He ordered powerful racing cars from Daimler and raced under the nickname "Mercedes," the name of his 11-year-old daughter, which means "grace" in Spanish. In 1901, the Mercedes 35 PS car made a big splash. In 1926, Daimler merged with Benz to become Daimler-Benz, and the name Mercedes-Benz was born.

cau_hoi: In 1955, British engineer Christopher Cockerell tested the idea of the hovercraft using what materials?
B: A cat food can placed in a coffee can, along with a blower
C: A wooden boat and an electric fan
giai_thich: Cockerell blew air into the space between two tin cans, then placed it on a kitchen scale to measure the lift force. He found that the air stream was "trapped" in a ring, creating much greater lift than blowing straight. The hovercraft rises on a cushion of air, able to travel over water, mud, and ice. In 1959, the SR.N1 hovercraft crossed the English Channel exactly 50 years after Blériot's flight.

cau_hoi: "Iron Lung," invented in 1928 by Philip Drinker and Louis Shaw, helped save thousands of people suffering from what disease?
C: Polio, when the disease paralyzes the respiratory muscles
giai_thich: Patients lay inside a sealed metal tube, with only their heads sticking out. A pump alternated the pressure inside the tube, causing the chest to expand and contract, helping air to flow in and out of the lungs. During polio outbreaks, hospitals had entire rooms filled with iron lungs. Thanks to the polio vaccine, the number of people needing the machines decreased significantly. Paul Alexander in the U.S. lived in an iron lung for over 70 years, passing away in 2024.

cau_hoi: In 1963, engineer Lou Ottens at Philips (Netherlands) invented the compact cassette tape. What size did he want the tape to be?
giai_thich: Previously, open reel tape recorders were very bulky and difficult to use. Ottens made a wooden block that fit in a jacket pocket to model the size. Philips allowed other companies to use the design for free, so the cassette tape became a global standard, selling billions of units. Ottens later contributed to the development of the CD. He passed away in 2021 at the age of 94.

cau_hoi: Chester Carlson invented the photocopying method (xerography) in 1938 in a small kitchen in New York. What did his first copy print?
C: "10-22-38 Astoria", the date and location of the experiment
giai_thich: Carlson worked in a patent office and had to hand-copy many documents while suffering from nearsightedness and arthritis. He used static electricity to attract colored powder to a metal plate, then transferred it to paper. Over 20 companies, including IBM, rejected the idea for many years. It wasn't until 1959 that the Xerox 914 photocopying machine was released and became a huge success, making Carlson very wealthy; he donated much of his fortune to charity.

cau_hoi: In 1957, two engineers Alfred Fielding and Marc Chavannes created bubble wrap. What did they initially intend to use it for?
giai_thich: The two men sealed two sheets of plastic together, trapping air bubbles, hoping to sell it as a new type of wallpaper, but no one bought it. They also tried to make insulation material for greenhouses but failed. By 1960, IBM used it to package new computers, and bubble wrap became a popular packaging material. The last Monday of January is "Bubble Wrap Appreciation Day."

cau_hoi: The toy "Silly Putty" was created during World War II when scientists were trying to create what?
B: Synthetic rubber to replace scarce natural rubber
giai_thich: Japanese forces occupied rubber plantations in Southeast Asia, so the U.S. needed synthetic rubber. In 1943, engineer James Wright at General Electric mixed boric acid with silicone oil, creating a strange substance: it bounced like a rubber ball, stretched when pulled, but broke when hit hard. It couldn't replace rubber, but in 1950 it was sold as a toy in plastic eggs. Apollo 8 astronauts even took Silly Putty into space to hold objects.

cau_hoi: In 2019, the ST25 rice variety from Vietnam was honored as the 'Best Rice in the World'. Which engineer's team in the old Soc Trang province developed this rice variety?
giai_thich: Engineer Ho Quang Cua and his colleagues spent over 20 years developing the fragrant ST rice variety (short for Soc Trang). ST25 has long grains, soft and sticky rice, a pandan aroma, and is resistant to saline soil. This rice variety won the Best Rice in the World competition held in the Philippines in 2019 and continued to achieve high awards in subsequent years. Soc Trang is now part of Can Tho city after the merger in 2025.

cau_hoi: Professor Vo Tong Xuan (1940 – 2024), an agronomist dedicated to rice cultivation in the Mekong Delta, was the first principal of which university?
B: Hanoi University of Science and Technology
giai_thich: He studied agriculture in the Philippines and Japan, worked at the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI), and then returned to contribute to bringing high-yield rice varieties to farmers in the Mekong region, helping Vietnam transition from rice shortage to a leading rice exporter. He often waded through rice fields with local farmers and was famous for his television program on rice cultivation techniques. In 1999, he became the first principal of An Giang University.

cau_hoi: In 1656, Dutch scientist Christiaan Huygens invented the first pendulum clock. How much more accurate was it compared to previous clocks?
A: The error decreased from about 15 minutes to about 15 seconds per day
B: The error increased to one hour per day
giai_thich: Galileo had noticed that each oscillation of the pendulum took almost the same amount of time, but Huygens was the one who turned that into a practical clock. The pendulum clock was the most accurate time-measuring device in the world until the 1930s. Huygens also attempted to create a pendulum clock for ships to determine longitude, but the rocking of the ship caused the clock to malfunction.

cau_hoi: In 1878, photographer Eadweard Muybridge used 12 cameras to take consecutive pictures of a horse running to answer which question?
A: How fast does the horse run
B: What colors can the horse see
C: Does the horse sleep standing up
D: Are there moments when all four of the horse's legs leave the ground
giai_thich: According to popular stories, Leland Stanford, the former governor of California, wanted to know the answer. The photos showed that there were moments when all four legs were off the ground, but this occurred when the legs were tucked under the belly, not extended forward and backward as artists usually depicted. By projecting the photos in sequence, Muybridge created moving images, an important step towards cinema.

cau_hoi: The film 'A Trip to the Moon' (1902) by French magician Georges Méliès is famous for which image?
C: A spaceship bullet embedded in the eye of 'Mr. Moon'
giai_thich: Méliès was a magician who discovered many cinematic tricks such as stopping the camera to make objects disappear, double exposure, and hand-coloring each frame. The film, about 13 minutes long, was very lengthy for that time, telling the story of astronomers shooting a giant bullet to the Moon, inspired by Jules Verne's novels. Méliès is considered the father of special effects in cinema.

cau_hoi: The film 'The Jazz Singer' (1927) marked what turning point in film history?
A: It was the first feature film with synchronized dialogue and singing with the images
B: It was the first animated film
C: It was the first color film
giai_thich: Previously, films were silent, with subtitles projected between scenes and musicians playing live in theaters. In the film, actor Al Jolson famously says: 'Wait, wait, you haven't heard anything yet!'. Just a few years later, silent films nearly disappeared, and many silent film stars lost their jobs because their voices did not match the talking films.

cau_hoi: The animated film 'Steamboat Willie' (1928), featuring Mickey Mouse, is famous for what?
B: One of the first animated films to have sound fully synchronized with the images
giai_thich: Walt Disney decided to make a sound film after seeing the success of talking films. Musicians recorded music according to the beats marked on the film so that the music and sound effects matched precisely with the movements. Mickey whistling while steering the boat became an iconic image. In 2024, the copyright of this film will expire in the U.S., making that first version of Mickey a public domain asset.

cau_hoi: The Telstar 1 satellite, launched on July 10, 1962, set what record in communication history?
C: The first photo of the Moon
D: The first live television images transmitted across the Atlantic
giai_thich: Telstar was a collaboration between AT&T, NASA, and European postal agencies. Because it orbited at a low altitude, it could only 'see' both shores of the Atlantic for about 20 minutes each time it passed overhead. The first program featured images of the Statue of Liberty, the Eiffel Tower, and a baseball game. In 1962, the song 'Telstar' by The Tornados topped the charts in both the UK and the US.

cau_hoi: Samuel Morse, who developed the telegraph and Morse code, was originally what profession before becoming an inventor?
giai_thich: In 1825, while Morse was painting a portrait of a general in Washington, he received a letter informing him that his wife was gravely ill. By the time he rushed home, she had passed away and was buried. The pain from the slow delivery of news drove him to find a faster way to communicate. In 1832, on a train journey back from Europe, he heard someone talking about electromagnets and came up with the idea for the telegraph.

cau_hoi: The codebreakers at Bletchley Park exploited a significant weakness in the Enigma machine. What was that weakness?
A: The machine revealed the password on the screen
B: The machine always encoded the same way each day
C: No letter was encoded as itself
giai_thich: Due to the wiring of the reflector, the letter A could never become A, the letter B could never become B... This allowed codebreakers to eliminate impossible positions when guessing a phrase that might appear in the message, such as 'weather report' or 'Heil Hitler'. The habits of German telegraph operators, such as often starting with the same phrase, also made decoding easier.

cau_hoi: In 2023, scientists at MIT announced a secret that helps ancient Roman concrete last for thousands of years. What is it?
A: Small lumps of quicklime in the concrete can 'self-heal' cracks when exposed to water
giai_thich: The Romans mixed lime with volcanic ash and water. Previously, the white lime spots in ancient concrete were thought to be due to poor mixing. Research shows that when water seeps into the cracks, it dissolves some calcium from the lime lumps, which then crystallizes and fills the cracks. This is why structures like the dome of the Pantheon in Rome have stood strong for nearly 1,900 years.

cau_hoi: The Lycurgus cup from Rome (4th century) has a strange color-changing ability: it appears green when light shines from the front and red when illuminated from within. Where is the secret?
B: A layer of water inside the cup
C: Gems attached to the surface of the cup
D: Tiny gold and silver nanoparticles mixed in the glass
giai_thich: The glass contains gold and silver particles that are only about 50 – 100 parts per million millimeters. At this size, the metals reflect and absorb light differently than usual, producing different colors depending on the angle of illumination. Scientists only understood this in 1990 using electron microscopy. Perhaps the Roman craftsman did not know why, but he created an ancient example of nanotechnology.

cau_hoi: Around 1297, the county magistrate Wang Zhen in China improved the movable type printing technique with wood to help typesetters work faster. How did he do it?
D: Placed over 60,000 characters on rotating tables, allowing the typesetter to sit in the middle and spin the table to select characters
giai_thich: Chinese characters have thousands of different characters, making movable type very time-consuming. Wang Zhen carved about 60,000 characters on wood, arranged alphabetically on two large rotating tables. The typesetter sat in the middle, simply spinning the table instead of walking around to find characters. He used this method to print a geographical book and documented the technique in the 'Agricultural Book'. Wooden movable type did not smudge ink like the earlier clay characters.

cau_hoi: The three brothers Banu Musa in Baghdad (9th century) described a machine considered one of the first 'programmable machines'. What was it?
A: An automatic flute-playing machine that plays music according to pins on a rotating drum that can be changed
giai_thich: In the 'Book of Ingenious Devices', the three brothers described about 100 machines, including a water-powered flute machine. The pins attached to a rotating drum open and close the flute holes in sequence; changing the drum changes the music, similar to changing a program. The brothers worked at the House of Wisdom (Bayt al-Hikma) in Baghdad, the largest academic center of that time.

cau_hoi: Around 1010, monk Eilmer at Malmesbury Abbey (England) is said to have flown about 200 meters with a homemade pair of wings. According to reports, he explained why he fell and broke his leg?
B: He forgot to attach a tail to the wings
giai_thich: According to historian William of Malmesbury, Eilmer jumped from the abbey tower and glided for a distance before falling, resulting in a lifelong limp. Similar to the story of Ibn Firnas, he realized that the tail was an important balancing component. He intended to try again but was forbidden by the abbot. Today, there is a stained glass window and a pub in Malmesbury commemorating the 'flying monk'.

cau_hoi: In 1858, French photographer Nadar took the first known aerial photograph. Where did he take it from?
C: From a hot air balloon flying over a village near Paris
D: From the top of the Eiffel Tower
giai_thich: Nadar had to bring a small darkroom up in the hot air balloon's basket, as photos at that time needed to be developed while the plate was still wet. He faced many failed attempts because the gas from the balloon damaged the chemicals. Unfortunately, the first photos were lost. Nadar also photographed most of the famous people of that time in Paris, and the Eiffel Tower was only built later, in 1889.

cau_hoi: In 1896, in England, Walter Arnold became one of the first people to be fined for speeding. How fast was he going?
A: About 13 km/h (8 mph), while the limit was about 3 km/h
giai_thich: According to the still-in-effect Red Flag Act, vehicles in town could only go about 2 mph. A policeman on a bicycle chased him down and caught him. Arnold was fined 1 shilling plus court costs. Interestingly, he was a car salesman for Benz, so the incident inadvertently helped advertise the car. Just a few months later, the law was relaxed, raising the limit to 14 mph.

cau_hoi: In 1911, engineer Charles Kettering invented the electric starter for cars, replacing the hand crank. What unfortunate event motivated him?
B: He broke his arm while driving
C: A friend of his, the owner of Cadillac, died after being struck by the hand crank
giai_thich: Previously, to start the engine, one had to crank the hand crank at the front of the car, and if the engine backfired, the crank could snap back and break an arm, even causing death. Kettering installed a small electric motor powered by a battery to turn the engine. From 1912, Cadillac cars had electric starters, making it easier for even those who lacked the strength to crank the engine to drive.

cau_hoi: In 1900, young engineer Ferdinand Porsche created the Lohner-Porsche. What made this car ahead of its time?
B: One of the first hybrid cars, with an electric motor mounted in the wheel and a gasoline engine for generating electricity
giai_thich: The first version ran entirely on electricity, with the motor placed directly in the wheel. Later, Porsche added a gasoline engine to run a generator, charging the battery, creating a 'hybrid' more than 100 years ago. Around 1900, electric cars were quite popular in America for being quiet, clean, and easy to start, until gasoline became cheap and electric starters made gasoline cars dominant.

cau_hoi: Obstetrician Ian Donald in Scotland developed medical ultrasound in the 1950s by borrowing which device?
C: A fish finder used by fishermen
D: A metal defect detector in shipyards
giai_thich: Donald had served in the air force and knew about radar and sonar. He brought tumors and body tissue to a boiler factory in Glasgow, tested the ultrasound waves of a weld inspection machine, and found that different tissues reflected different waves. In 1958, he published a famous paper on ultrasound diagnosis. Today, prenatal ultrasound is the first image many families see of their baby.

cau_hoi: In 1924, German psychiatrist Hans Berger recorded what type of signal from a person for the first time?
giai_thich: Berger believed there was a form of "spiritual energy" transmitted between people, and to find it, he began measuring electricity on the scalp. He discovered rhythmic electrical oscillations of about 10 times per second when a person relaxed with their eyes closed, now called alpha waves. The discovery was met with skepticism for many years, but today EEG is used to diagnose epilepsy, study sleep, and brain function.

cau_hoi: In 1953, American doctor John Gibbon successfully used a heart-lung machine in surgery for the first time. What does this machine do?
A: Temporarily takes over blood pumping and oxygen supply, allowing the surgeon to operate on a stopped heart
giai_thich: Gibbon spent nearly 20 years developing the machine, initially testing it on cats with his wife Mary Hopkinson. In 1953, he used the machine on 18-year-old Cecelia Bavolek for about 26 minutes to patch a hole in the heart wall. The successful surgery opened the era of open-heart surgery. Some of the first machines were built with the help of IBM.

cau_hoi: In 1943, when American scientists were looking for a type of mold that produced more penicillin for mass production, where was the best strain found?
B: On a piece of bread in London
C: At the bottom of the deep sea
D: On a moldy cantaloupe at the Peoria city market (Illinois)
giai_thich: The laboratory in Peoria asked people, pilots, and soldiers around the world to send mold samples. An employee known as "Moldy Mary" specialized in shopping for spoiled fruits. The strain on the cantaloupe produced many times more penicillin than Fleming's original strain, and after being X-rayed to induce mutations, it was even better. Thanks to this, by the time of the Normandy landings in 1944, millions of doses of penicillin were available.

cau_hoi: British scientist William Henry Fox Talbot created a photography method that had what significant difference compared to the daguerreotype method?
B: Created a negative plate from which multiple identical photos could be printed
C: Took photos in a few minutes on metal
giai_thich: Each daguerreotype was a unique photo that could not be copied. Talbot created negative images on paper, with reversed light and dark, and then printed onto another paper to get positive images. The oldest surviving negative is a picture of a window in his home, Lacock Abbey, taken in 1835. The method of taking negatives and then printing positives was used for over 150 years, until the advent of digital cameras.

cau_hoi: Almon Strowger, who invented the automatic telephone exchange between 1889 and 1891, worked in what profession and why did he want to eliminate the human operator?
A: Doctor, because he needed to make calls quickly
B: Funeral home owner, because he suspected the operator was redirecting calls to a competitor
C: Electrician, because he wanted more work
D: Teacher, because he wanted to teach students
giai_thich: At that time, to make a call, one had to rely on the operator to connect the lines. According to the famous story, the wife of one of Strowger's competitors worked as an operator and redirected calls looking for "the funeral home" to her husband. Strowger was angry and invented an automatic switching system based on dialed numbers. This type of exchange was used in many places until the end of the 20th century.

cau_hoi: The IBM Simon, released in 1994, is often regarded as what?
C: The first "smartphone", with a touchscreen, email, calendar, and the ability to install additional applications
giai_thich: Simon weighed about 0.5 kg, had a battery life of only about one hour, and cost around $900. Users could send faxes, emails, and take notes with a stylus. The term "smartphone" was not yet popular at that time. Only about 50,000 units were sold before production ceased, but Simon had almost all the features that later smartphones developed.

cau_hoi: What was the first item sold on the eBay auction site in 1995?
giai_thich: Founder Pierre Omidyar listed a broken laser pointer to test the website and was surprised when someone bought it for $14.83. He contacted the buyer to ensure they knew the pointer was broken; the buyer replied that he was a "collector of broken laser pointers". The story illustrates how the Internet can connect people with very niche interests.

cau_hoi: On May 22, 2010, programmer Laszlo Hanyecz used 10,000 bitcoins to buy what, now remembered annually as "Bitcoin Pizza Day"?
giai_thich: This was one of the first times bitcoin was used to purchase real goods. At that time, 10,000 bitcoins were worth about $40. A few years later, that amount of bitcoin was valued at hundreds of millions of dollars, then over a billion dollars. Bitcoin was created in 2009 by a person or group using the name Satoshi Nakamoto, and Satoshi's true identity remains a mystery to this day.

cau_hoi: Between 1983 and 1986, engineer Chuck Hull invented the first patented 3D printing technology, called "stereolithography". How does this technology work?
A: Cuts wood with a laser beam
B: Projects ultraviolet light to harden layers of liquid plastic, stacking them to form an object
D: Pours molten metal into a mold
giai_thich: Hull worked at a company that produced UV-cured coatings for tabletops. He realized that light could be used to harden thin layers of plastic according to a computer design. According to him, the first object he printed was a small black eye wash cup. He also created the STL file format, which is still used by most 3D printers today.

cau_hoi: When developing the MP3 music compression format, engineer Karlheinz Brandenburg at the Fraunhofer Institute (Germany) repeatedly used which song for testing, as its raw vocal was very difficult to compress without distortion?
giai_thich: MP3 removes parts of the sound that are difficult for the human ear to hear, reducing the file size by about 10 times. Brandenburg listened to this nearly a cappella song hundreds of times to fine-tune the algorithm, to the point where Suzanne Vega was jokingly called the "mother of MP3". MP3 made listening to music online and on portable music players popular from the late 1990s.

cau_hoi: In 1969, engineer Bob Gore accidentally invented the waterproof yet breathable fabric Gore-Tex. How did he do it?
C: Pulling a heated PTFE plastic rod quickly and forcefully, causing it to expand many times and create tiny holes
giai_thich: Pulling slowly causes PTFE (the material used in non-stick pans) to break, but pulling quickly allows it to stretch about 800% into a porous membrane. The tiny holes in the membrane are thousands of times smaller than a water droplet, so rain does not penetrate, but larger than water vapor molecules, allowing sweat to escape. Gore-Tex fabric is used for mountaineering jackets, astronaut gear, and even in medicine like artificial blood vessels.

cau_hoi: How did physicist Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit, who created the first accurate mercury thermometer (1714), choose the zero point of the temperature scale named after him?
A: The temperature of a mixture of ice water and ammonium chloride
B: The freezing temperature of pure water
C: The coldest temperature in the Arctic
giai_thich: Fahrenheit wanted to avoid negative numbers during the coldest winter days in Europe, so he chose the coldest temperature he could create in the laboratory as 0°F. The second reference point was initially the human body temperature, around 96°F, which was later adjusted. On this scale, water freezes at 32°F and boils at 212°F. Today, Fahrenheit is still primarily used in daily life in the United States.

cau_hoi: In 1853, doctor Alexander Wood in Scotland and doctor Charles Pravaz in France almost simultaneously developed which medical instrument?
A: A syringe with a hollow needle for injecting drugs through the skin
giai_thich: Previously, medicines were mainly taken orally, applied, or placed on cuts. The sharp hollow needle could accurately deliver medicine deep under the skin. It is said that Wood was inspired by the stinger of a bee. Today, tens of billions of injections are performed each year worldwide, and disposable syringes were introduced in the mid-20th century to help prevent disease transmission.

cau_hoi: In 1867, doctor Thomas Clifford Allbutt in England created the handheld medical thermometer. What made it much more convenient than previous thermometers?
B: Only about 15 cm long and measures body temperature in about 5 minutes
giai_thich: Previous medical thermometers were about 30 cm long and took up to 20 minutes to measure, so few doctors used them. Allbutt's small thermometer made measuring body temperature a routine practice in examinations. Today, electronic and infrared thermometers provide results in just a few seconds, and mercury thermometers are gradually being phased out due to the toxicity of mercury.

cau_hoi: In 1965, engineer E.A. Johnson in England described the first capacitive touch screen, a type of screen used in today's smartphones. What was it originally developed for?
giai_thich: Johnson worked at the Royal Radar Institute in Malvern. He wanted controllers to touch the radar screen directly to select aircraft instead of typing commands. The capacitive touch screen works because the human body conducts electricity, so a finger alters the electric field on the glass surface. That's why wearing wool gloves usually prevents touching the phone screen.

cau_hoi: In 2004, the U.S. military research agency DARPA held a competition for self-driving cars to traverse about 240 km of desert. What was the result?
A: All vehicles finished within an hour
B: A car flew over the desert
C: No vehicle finished; the farthest any vehicle went was about 12 km
giai_thich: The prize was $1 million, but many vehicles flipped, got stuck, or went off course within minutes. Just a year later, in 2005, five vehicles completed the race, and Stanford University's Stanley won. Many engineers who participated in these competitions later became leaders of self-driving car projects at Google and many other companies.

cau_hoi: In 1888, inventor Charles Brush in Cleveland (USA) created one of the first automatic wind turbines for electricity generation. What was it used for?
A: To provide electricity for his house, charging dozens of batteries
D: To pump water for the entire city
giai_thich: Brush's turbine was about 18 m tall, had 144 cedar wood blades, and generated about 12 kW, charging about 400 batteries in the basement. His house had electric lights and electric motors, making it one of the most modern homes of its time. The turbine operated for about 20 years. Today, modern wind turbines only have 3 blades but are massive, each generating several million watts.

cau_hoi: Where did the world's first nuclear power plant supplying electricity to the national grid begin operations in 1954?
giai_thich: The plant in Obninsk, near Moscow, had a capacity of about 5 MW, enough for a few thousand households, and was called the "Peaceful Nuclear Power Plant." It operated until 2002 and then became a museum. The world's first nuclear reactor, Chicago Pile-1 (1942), was just an experimental reactor and did not generate electricity. In 1956, the Calder Hall plant in England became the first large-scale commercial nuclear power plant.

cau_hoi: In 1955, British physicist Louis Essen created the first accurate atomic clock using atoms of which element?
giai_thich: Atomic clocks count the oscillations of cesium atoms, which are always identical everywhere. In 1967, the second was redefined based on cesium: one second is about 9.19 billion oscillations. Essen's clock was off by about 1 second in 300 years, while today's atomic clocks are off by less than 1 second in billions of years. GPS systems and the Internet both rely on atomic clocks.

cau_hoi: In 1896, Italian doctor Scipione Riva-Rocci invented which medical device that is now found in almost every clinic?
C: Blood pressure monitor with a cuff wrapped around the arm
giai_thich: The cuff is inflated to compress the arm's artery, then slowly deflates, with a mercury column indicating blood pressure. In 1905, Russian doctor Nikolai Korotkov discovered that a stethoscope could be used to hear the heartbeat, helping to measure both systolic and diastolic blood pressure. Therefore, blood pressure is still recorded in the unit of "millimeters of mercury" (mmHg) to this day.

cau_hoi: "The bifurcated needle," invented in 1965 by Benjamin Rubin, played a crucial role in which campaign?
C: The global eradication campaign of smallpox
giai_thich: The needle has two sharp points like a small fork, holding exactly one drop of vaccine between the two points due to surface tension. The injector only needs to prick the skin about 15 times. The needle is very cheap, easy to use, can be sterilized and reused, and saves vaccine four times. As a result, healthcare workers vaccinated hundreds of millions of people, and by 1980, smallpox was declared completely eradicated.

cau_hoi: In 1941, due to a lack of equipment to grow enough fungi to produce penicillin, scientist Norman Heatley at Oxford University used what items?
D: Hospital bedpans, bathtubs, milk bottles, and cake boxes
giai_thich: During wartime, Howard Florey and Ernst Chain's team needed large amounts of penicillin for human trials. Heatley designed shallow ceramic jars resembling bedpans and hired young girls to care for the fungi (known as "penicillin girls"). He also devised a method to extract penicillin from the fungal broth. Despite his significant contributions, Heatley was not awarded the Nobel Prize in 1945 alongside Fleming, Florey, and Chain.

cau_hoi: The VinFuture Prize of Vietnam awarded its first Grand Prize in 2021 to whom?
B: Scientists who laid the foundation for mRNA vaccine technology, such as Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman
C: The inventor of the mobile phone
D: The scientist who discovered water on Mars
giai_thich: The VinFuture Prize was established in 2020 with a Grand Prize worth 3 million dollars, among the largest scientific awards in the world. The first award was given to Katalin Karikó, Drew Weissman, and Pieter Cullis, who contributed to mRNA technology and lipid nanoparticles, facilitating the rapid development of COVID-19 vaccines. Two years later, Karikó and Weissman received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2023.

cau_hoi: Professor Hoàng Tụy (1927 – 2019), a Vietnamese mathematician, is world-renowned for which work?
A: Laying the foundation for global optimization theory with the "Tụy cut" method
giai_thich: In 1964, Hoàng Tụy published the cutting method to find the best solutions for problems with many "local good points" causing interference, known in mathematics as the "Tụy cut." The field of global optimization helps solve complex design, economic, and engineering problems. He also contributed to the establishment of the Vietnam Institute of Mathematics and provided many suggestions for education.

cau_hoi: In 1977, an engineer from Canon (Japan) accidentally discovered the principle of thermal inkjet printing while doing what?
A: Blowing up balloons filled with ink
B: Pouring water into a laser printer
C: Accidentally placing a hot soldering iron on the tip of an ink-filled syringe, causing the ink to spray out
D: Dropping a fountain pen on the floor
giai_thich: The heat caused a small amount of ink to boil, creating tiny bubbles that pushed a droplet of ink out of the nozzle. From there, Canon developed the "bubble jet" technology: the print head has hundreds of tiny tubes, each with a resistor that heats up in microseconds to shoot ink. Around the same time, Hewlett-Packard in the U.S. also independently developed similar technology.

cau_hoi: The Kinetoscope, developed by Edison and engineer William Dickson in the early 1890s, allowed films to be viewed in what way?
B: Projected onto a large screen for the whole theater
D: Each person looked through a small hole in a wooden box
giai_thich: The film ran continuously through a light bulb inside the box, and viewers dropped a coin and leaned down to watch short scenes of about a few dozen seconds, such as dancers, athletes, and boxers. In 1894, "Kinetoscope parlors" opened in New York. Edison initially thought projecting films for the entire theater would be less profitable, so he lagged behind the Lumière brothers.

cau_hoi: The "zoetrope" toy popular in the 19th century creates the illusion of motion in what way, similar to the principle of animation?
A: A round drum with slits spins quickly, revealing successive drawings inside as if they are moving
giai_thich: As the drum spins, the eye looking through the slit sees each image for just a moment before being blocked, so the successive drawings appear as a galloping horse or a jumping rope. The eye and brain "hold" each image for a moment and connect them into motion. The Vietnamese 'đèn kéo quân,' with figures revolving around a candle, also creates a similar illusion of movement.

cau_hoi: In 1878, Emma Nutt in Boston (USA) became the first woman to do what job, earning $10 a month?
giai_thich: Initially, telephone companies hired young men to operate switchboards, but they were often rude to customers and played pranks. Emma Nutt was recruited by Alexander Graham Bell and became famous for her gentle voice and good memory for phone numbers. Later, companies began hiring women. She worked for 33 years, and the switchboard operator profession became one of the most common jobs for women at that time.

cau_hoi: The word "Hello" became the greeting when picking up the phone thanks to whom's suggestion? And Alexander Graham Bell wanted to use what word?
A: Morse suggested "Hello"; Bell wanted to use "Good day"
B: Marconi suggested "Hello"; Edison wanted to use "Yes"
C: Bell suggested "Hello"; Edison wanted to use "Hi"
D: Thomas Edison suggested "Hello"; Bell wanted to use "Ahoy"
giai_thich: Edison wrote in 1877 that "Hello" was the appropriate word to call when someone was on the other end of the line. Bell preferred "Ahoy!", the sailor's greeting, and used it until the end of his life. The first telephone directories even instructed users on how to start and end a call, as talking over the phone was a completely new experience.

cau_hoi: In 1858, the first transatlantic telegraph cable was completed, and Queen Victoria sent a congratulatory message to the President of the United States. What happened?
A: The 98-word message took about 16 hours to transmit, and only about three weeks later the cable completely failed
B: The message arrived immediately and the cable lasted for 100 years
C: A whale bit through the cable on the first day
D: The message was mistakenly sent to Russia
giai_thich: The signal through the over 3,000 km long cable was very weak and distorted, so each letter had to be sent very slowly. An engineer increased the voltage very high to try to strengthen the signal, and the cable was damaged. It wasn't until 1866 that the giant ship Great Eastern successfully laid a sustainable cable. Today, about 99% of Internet data between continents travels through underwater fiber optic cables.

cau_hoi: In 1888, Theophilus Van Kannel in Philadelphia was granted a patent for the revolving door. According to a story, why did he invent it?
B: He was making toys for his child
C: He hated holding the door for others out of politeness
giai_thich: Aside from that amusing story, revolving doors have real benefits: they always remain 'closed', preventing cold winds, dust, and noise from entering the building, and reducing the chimney effect in high-rise buildings when warm air rises, making doors difficult to open. A study at MIT showed that using revolving doors instead of regular doors can significantly save heating energy.

cau_hoi: In 1934, British inventor Percy Shaw created the 'cat's eye' road marker to reflect car headlights at night. According to the famous story, where did he get his inspiration?
B: The reflected light from a cat's eyes on a fence while he was driving in fog
giai_thich: Shaw's cat's eyes consist of round glass beads set in a rubber casing. When a car passes, the rubber casing is pressed down, and rainwater underneath cleans the 'eye', just like a cat blinking. During World War II, when cities had to turn off lights to avoid enemy planes, cat's eyes helped vehicles travel safely, and Shaw became wealthy.

cau_hoi: In 1937, Sylvan Goldman, owner of a supermarket chain in Oklahoma (USA), invented the shopping cart. Initially, customers refused to use it, so what did he do?
A: Punished customers for not using the cart
C: Gave carts to customers to take home
D: Hired people to pretend to be customers pushing carts in the store
giai_thich: Goldman combined two baskets on a folding chair frame with wheels. However, men felt that pushing a cart was unmanly, while women thought it resembled a baby stroller. When they saw many 'customers' pushing carts, people began to follow suit. The cart helped customers buy more items, contributing to the growth of supermarkets as we know them today.

cau_hoi: The transparent tape 'Scotch tape' was invented by engineer Richard Drew at 3M in 1930. Where does the name 'Scotch' come from?
A: A customer complained that the company was 'stingy' like Scotsmen for applying too little adhesive on the tape before
B: The name of a type of whiskey
D: The name of an island in Scotland
giai_thich: In 1925, Drew created masking tape for auto painters to cover areas that didn't need painting. The test batch only had adhesive on the edges to save costs, and the tape peeled off, frustrating the workers. The phrase 'Scotch stinginess' was a stereotype at the time, but the name stuck with the product. During the Great Depression, people used tape to repair items instead of buying new ones.

cau_hoi: Water-resistant duct tape was developed during World War II thanks to a letter from whom sent to President Roosevelt?
C: Vesta Stoudt, a munitions factory worker with two sons in the Navy
giai_thich: Stoudt saw ammunition boxes sealed with paper tape that had a pull tab, but the paper tape was very difficult to tear when wet, wasting valuable time for soldiers. She proposed using water-resistant cloth tape and wrote a letter to the President. He forwarded the letter to the War Production Board, and Johnson & Johnson produced the new tape. Soldiers used it to fix everything from boots to jeeps.

cau_hoi: What does the name of the famous rust prevention and lubricant solution 'WD-40' (1953) mean?
B: 'Water Displacement, 40th formula': the 40th formula to displace water, after 39 failed attempts
giai_thich: Rocket Chemical Company in San Diego (USA) needed a rust preventative for the Atlas rocket's casing. After 39 failed attempts, the 40th formula succeeded. Employees secretly took it home and found it great for bicycles, door hinges, and tools, so in 1958 the product was sold in stores. The exact ingredients remain a trade secret to this day.

cau_hoi: Bette Nesmith Graham, a typist, invented Liquid Paper in 1956. What did her son later become famous for?
B: A member of the band The Monkees
D: An astronaut who went to the Moon
giai_thich: She observed window decorators painting over mistakes instead of erasing them, so she mixed white water-based paint in her kitchen to cover typing errors. She was fired for a mistake she couldn't fix, then focused on marketing the product. In 1979, she sold the company for about $47.5 million. Her son, Michael Nesmith, became a member of the pop band The Monkees.

cau_hoi: The 'cut, copy, and paste' operation on computers became popular thanks to which computer scientist working at Xerox PARC in the 1970s?
giai_thich: Tesler believed that computers should be easy for ordinary people to use, without needing to remember complex commands. He also opposed 'modes' in software, and his license plate read 'NO MODES'. Later, he worked for Apple, contributing to the design of the Lisa and Macintosh computers. The cut and paste operation was inspired by editors cutting and pasting paper to rearrange articles.

cau_hoi: The first website in the world, created by Tim Berners-Lee in 1991 and still accessible today, is about what?
C: Introducing the World Wide Web project and how to use it
giai_thich: The site was hosted on Berners-Lee's NeXT computer at CERN, which had a label saying 'This machine is a server. DO NOT TURN IT OFF!!'. The page explained what the World Wide Web was, how to create a web page, and how to use a browser. In 2013, CERN restored the original website at info.cern.ch. In 1993, CERN announced that everyone could use web technology for free, leading to the web explosion.

cau_hoi: Where does the name of the company 'Sony', established in 1958, come from?
B: The name of a city in Japan
D: A combination of 'sonus' (sound, Latin) and 'sonny' (boy, English), representing a group of energetic young people
giai_thich: The company's original name was Tokyo Tsushin Kogyo (Tokyo Telecommunications Engineering Corporation), which was too long and difficult for foreigners to pronounce. Founders Masaru Ibuka and Akio Morita wanted a short, memorable name in all languages. In 1955, the company launched the TR-55 transistor radio, one of the first transistor radios in Japan.

cau_hoi: In 1924, Sakichi Toyoda, the founder of the later Toyota group, invented an automatic loom with what special feature that became an important principle of production?
A: Automatically stops when a thread breaks, preventing defective fabric from being woven
D: Does not require a human operator forever
giai_thich: This principle is called "jidoka", meaning the machine automatically detects faults and stops for humans to fix, rather than continuing to produce defective goods. Toyoda sold the patent for the loom to a British company, and his son, Kiichiro, used the money to start car production. The Toyota production method was later adopted by factories around the world.

cau_hoi: The company Nokia, once the largest mobile phone manufacturer in the world, was founded in 1865 in Finland to produce what?
giai_thich: Engineer Fredrik Idestam opened a paper mill by the river, and the name Nokia was taken from the town where the second mill was located. Over more than 100 years, Nokia produced rubber boots, tires, electrical cables, and televisions before focusing on mobile phones. The Nokia 3310, launched in 2000, became famous for being "indestructible" and featured the game Snake.

cau_hoi: In 1884, German student Paul Nipkow was granted a patent for a component later used in the first mechanical televisions. What was it?
D: A rotating disk with small holes arranged in a spiral to scan images line by line
giai_thich: Nipkow conceived this idea on Christmas Eve when he was just 23 years old. As the disk rotated, each hole scanned a line of the image, and the light passing through the hole was converted into an electrical signal. He never built a working system, and the patent expired. More than 40 years later, John Logie Baird used Nipkow's disk to transmit the first television images.

cau_hoi: In 1947, two Bell Labs engineers, Douglas Ring and Rae Young, proposed what idea that later became the foundation of mobile phone networks?
A: Running telephone wires to each person
C: Dividing coverage areas into hexagonal "cells", each with its own transmitter and reusing frequencies in distant cells
D: Using laser light to make calls
giai_thich: Instead of a giant antenna covering the entire city with a limited number of channels, many small stations with narrow coverage could reuse the same frequency in distant cells, serving millions of people. This is why mobile phones are called "cell phones" in English. However, it took more than 30 years for the technology to switch calls between cells to be good enough for mobile networks to become a reality.

cau_hoi: The world's first parking meter was installed in 1935 in which city?
giai_thich: With the increasing number of cars, central streets were occupied all day, leaving no parking for shoppers. Journalist Carl Magee proposed a coin-operated meter to limit parking time. Upon installation, some residents protested vehemently, even suing. But shop owners liked it because it increased customer turnover, and parking meters quickly spread around the world.

cau_hoi: In 1916, the Piggly Wiggly store in Memphis (USA) introduced a new way of selling that is now very familiar. What was it?
D: Self-service store: customers take items from the shelves and pay at the checkout
giai_thich: Previously, customers handed a list to staff, who retrieved items from behind the counter. Clarence Saunders allowed customers to walk through aisles of shelves with marked prices, selecting items themselves. This method reduced labor costs and helped lower prices. He was granted a patent for the "self-service store" model. The name Piggly Wiggly is said to have been chosen to pique curiosity and be memorable.

cau_hoi: In 1979, student Dan Bricklin and programmer Bob Frankston created VisiCalc, the first electronic spreadsheet for personal computers. What impact did it have?
A: Caused many businesses to buy Apple II computers just to use this program
giai_thich: Bricklin saw a teacher at Harvard Business School having to erase and recalculate an entire number table on the blackboard every time a single number changed. He envisioned a spreadsheet on a screen that would update automatically. VisiCalc was called the first "killer app", so compelling that people bought entire computers just to use it. They were not granted a patent because the laws at the time did not protect software.

cau_hoi: In 1963, Ted Nelson coined what term, the idea of linked text allowing jumps from one document to another, the foundation of web pages?
giai_thich: Since 1960, Nelson began the Xanadu Project, an imagined system where every document in the world was linked, had a history of modifications, and automatically paid royalties to authors. The project was never completed as he envisioned. However, his idea of hypertext influenced Tim Berners-Lee when creating the World Wide Web, where each link is a "hyperlink".

cau_hoi: The software for the Apollo guidance computer was stored in "core rope memory". How was this memory made?
B: Workers, mostly women, threaded copper wire through or around magnetic cores by hand
giai_thich: Each bit of information is a 1 or 0 depending on whether the wire passes through the magnetic core or loops around it. Female workers, many of whom had previously worked in textile mills, took weeks to "weave" a program. Engineers jokingly called it the "LOL" (little old ladies) method. This memory was extremely durable and could not be erased, making it very suitable for the critical flight to the Moon.

cau_hoi: "Spacewar!" (1962), created by a group of students at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), is what type of game?
C: A two-player game controlling two spaceships shooting at each other, orbiting a star with gravitational pull
giai_thich: Steve Russell and his friends wrote the game on the school's expensive PDP-1 computer, which included the gravitational force of the star in the center of the screen pulling the ships in. Because laboratory computers were very rare, the game spread to many universities via punched paper tape. Spacewar! is one of the earliest video games with a wide influence, inspiring the first commercial arcade games.

cau_hoi: In 1992, the photo considered to be one of the first images posted on the World Wide Web was of whom?
D: The female band "Les Horribles Cernettes" consisting of CERN staff
giai_thich: This fun band sang songs about particle physics. A colleague took a photo of the group, and Berners-Lee suggested posting one on the website to test the image display feature. The photo was edited with early graphic software. The band's acronym, LHC, coincides with the name of CERN's large particle accelerator.

cau_hoi: In 1996, the USB connection standard was introduced to make it easier to connect devices to computers. Which engineer at Intel is often mentioned as the leader in USB development?
giai_thich: Before USB, computers had various ports for mice, keyboards, printers, and installing new devices was often quite complicated. Bhatt and colleagues from various companies designed a universal "plug and play" port. Intel did not charge royalties, so USB spread worldwide. In 2009, an Intel advertisement even turned him into the "rock star" of the tech world. Today's USB-C ports can be plugged in either way.

cau_hoi: Which type of memory did engineer Fujio Masuoka at Toshiba invent in the 1980s, now found in USBs, memory cards, and phones?
giai_thich: Flash memory retains data even when power is lost and can erase a large block of data very quickly. A colleague of Masuoka named it "flash" because the data erasure reminded him of a camera flash. According to reports, Masuoka received only a small bonus from Toshiba, later sued the company, and received about 87 million yen in compensation in 2006.

cau_hoi: In 1969, Willard Boyle and George Smith at Bell Labs invented the CCD sensor, which earned them half of the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2009. How long did they reportedly sketch this idea?
D: About an hour on a blackboard
giai_thich: The CCD sensor converts light into electrical signals, with each pixel passing charge to the next like a chain passing a bucket of water. Initially, they intended to create computer memory, but the CCD became the "eyes" of digital cameras, the Hubble telescope, and camcorders. The other half of the 2009 Nobel Prize was awarded to Charles Kao for fiber optics.

cau_hoi: What was the shape of the first escalator in the U.S., installed in 1896 at Coney Island amusement park (New York)?
B: An inclined conveyor belt with a rail, without steps, like an "inclined elevator"
giai_thich: Inventor Jesse Reno created the "inclined conveyor" which was only about 2 meters high, like a fun ride. About 75,000 people tried it out in two weeks. The term "escalator" later became the trademark of Otis, derived from "scala" (step, Latin) and "elevator". Today, the longest outdoor escalator with a roof in the world is in Hong Kong, measuring about 800 meters.

cau_hoi: In 1973, a U.S. federal court ruled that the ENIAC patent was invalid. The reason was that the idea of a digital electronic computer had been proposed by whom before?
A: John Atanasoff, who along with student Clifford Berry built the ABC computer in Iowa
giai_thich: The Atanasoff-Berry Computer (ABC), built around 1939-1942, used vacuum tubes and binary to solve equations but was not programmable. One of the ENIAC creators, John Mauchly, visited Atanasoff and saw the machine in 1941. The ruling made the idea of electronic computers public domain, with no company holding a monopoly.

cau_hoi: "Stigler's Law" (1980) makes a humorous observation about the history of science. What does it state?
C: No scientific discovery is named after the person who actually discovered it first
D: All inventions are created on a Monday
giai_thich: Statistician Stephen Stigler made this remark, humorously noting that the idea is actually from sociologist Robert Merton. There are many examples: Halley's comet has been recorded since ancient times, and America is named after Amerigo Vespucci rather than the first person to arrive. The law reminds us that science is a collective effort of many people.

cau_hoi: In 1890, Edison sold what type of toy, considered one of his biggest failures because it frightened children?
D: Talking doll with a tiny phonograph inside
giai_thich: Each doll had a small phonograph with a record of a nursery rhyme, made by girls working in the recording studio. However, the sound was scratchy and shrill, the machine was prone to breaking, and the dolls were heavy and expensive. Just a few weeks later, Edison stopped selling them. In 2015, scientists used optical scanning technology to replay these old recordings without damaging them.

cau_hoi: The Wardenclyffe Tower on Long Island (New York), built in the early 20th century, was Nikola Tesla's ambitious project aimed at what?
B: Transmitting signals and electrical energy wirelessly around the world
giai_thich: Tesla believed it was possible to use the Earth itself and the atmosphere to transmit electricity and information over long distances without wires. Financier J.P. Morgan initially funded it but withdrew, perhaps because he saw no profit in "free" energy, while Marconi had already sent signals across the Atlantic. The tower was demolished in 1917. Today, the site has become a museum about Tesla.

cau_hoi: In 1880, Alexander Graham Bell and assistant Charles Tainter invented the "photophone", which Bell considered his most important invention. What does it do?
A: Transmits voice using a beam of light, without wires
giai_thich: Voice vibrations caused a thin mirror to vibrate, modulating the light beam according to the sound. At the other end, a selenium cell converted the changing light into an electric current and then into sound. The photophone only worked in clear weather and over short distances, so it was not widely adopted. However, the principle of transmitting information using light is the ancestor of today's fiber optics.

cau_hoi: The first electric tattoo machine, patented by Samuel O'Reilly in 1891, was developed based on which of Edison's inventions?
A: An electric pen used to punch holes in paper for printing templates
giai_thich: "Edison's pen" (1876) had a small needle powered by an electric motor that punched tiny holes in paper according to the handwriting, which was then used as a mold to print multiple copies. The product was not very successful. O'Reilly, a tattoo artist in New York, added an ink tube and adjusted the needle to inject ink into the skin much faster than hand tattooing. His basic design is still in use today.

cau_hoi: In 1869, George Westinghouse invented the air brake for trains. How were trains braked before that?
B: The brakeman had to run on top of the cars and manually apply the brakes one car at a time
C: The engineer dropped an anchor onto the tracks
D: The train stopped by itself when it ran out of coal
giai_thich: The job of a brakeman was very dangerous, especially in rain, snow, or at night, and many fell to their deaths. Westinghouse's air brake allowed the engineer to brake all cars at once from the locomotive using compressed air. The improved version even applied the brakes automatically if the cars became separated. As a result, trains could run faster, longer, and much safer.

cau_hoi: In 1890, Herman Hollerith used a punch card reader to process the U.S. census. What company did he later establish that became a major corporation?
giai_thich: The 1880 census took about 8 years to count by hand. With Hollerith's machine, each citizen was recorded by holes on a card, and the machine counted by allowing a needle to touch through the holes into a mercury cup to complete the circuit. Preliminary results were available in a few weeks, and the entire count was much faster than before. In 1924, his merged company was renamed International Business Machines (IBM).

cau_hoi: In 1942, the Daily Telegraph in England held a crossword puzzle competition. What special invitation did the fastest solvers later receive?
D: To work secretly at Bletchley Park to decode German codes
giai_thich: The challenge was to solve the newspaper's crossword in 12 minutes. Some completed it and were later contacted by the War Department to work on codebreaking. Bletchley Park recruited people from various backgrounds, such as mathematicians, linguists, chess players, and crossword solvers, as they needed sharp minds to recognize patterns. Most kept their work secret for decades.

cau_hoi: "The Mechanical Turk," a famous chess-playing machine built in 1770, defeated both Napoleon and Benjamin Franklin. What was its real secret?
A: It used water power to think
B: A skilled player hid inside the cabinet controlling the moves
C: It was the first electronic computer
D: It was controlled by remote magnets from the audience
giai_thich: Engineer Wolfgang von Kempelen built the machine to impress Empress Maria Theresa of Austria. He opened the cabinet doors for the audience to see all the gears, but a chess player could skillfully move inside. The secret was only revealed decades later. Today, the name "Mechanical Turk" is used for a service that hires people to do small tasks that computers cannot yet perform well.

cau_hoi: "The Digesting Duck" demonstrated by French inventor Jacques de Vaucanson in 1739 is famous for doing what, even though it was actually a trick?
D: Eating grains, then "digesting" and excreting them
giai_thich: The mechanical duck made of gilded copper had over 400 moving parts, could flap its wings, drink water, and peck at grains. The audience was astonished when it "went to the bathroom." In reality, the excrement was pre-stored in a hidden compartment. Nevertheless, Vaucanson was a brilliant engineer: he also created flute-playing automatons and an automatic loom, which was later improved by Jacquard.

cau_hoi: In 1919, the HD-4 hydrofoil boat built by Alexander Graham Bell and engineer Casey Baldwin set what record?
C: World speed record on water, about 114 km/h
D: Fastest crossing of the Atlantic Ocean
giai_thich: The hydrofoil boat had "wings" underwater that lifted the hull out of the water when running fast, greatly reducing drag. Bell, then over 70 years old, worked with associates at Bras d'Or Lake (Canada), where he had a summer home. The HD-4's record stood for about 10 years. Besides the telephone, Bell also researched kites, airplanes, and medical devices.

cau_hoi: How did the pneumatic post system in Paris, operating from 1866 to 1984, work?
A: Letters were placed in small tubes and pushed through a network of underground tubes hundreds of kilometers long using compressed air
giai_thich: The underground tube network in Paris was at one point nearly 470 km long, connecting post offices throughout the city. The "petit bleu" (small blue letters) could reach recipients in about two hours. Similar systems existed in many cities like London, Berlin, and Prague. Today, many hospitals still use pneumatic tubes to send test samples between departments.

cau_hoi: In 1971, musician Daisuke Inoue in Kobe (Japan) created the "8 Juke" karaoke machine for customers to sing along with the background music. What was special about his invention?
A: He did not register a patent, so he did not earn royalties, but later received the Ig Nobel Peace Prize in 2004
B: The machine was banned by the government
C: The machine could only play one song
D: He became the richest person in Japan
giai_thich: Karaoke means "empty orchestra": "kara" is empty, "oke" is short for orchestra. Inoue often accompanied customers singing at a bar, so he recorded the accompaniment for customers to sing when he was absent. He rented out the machine instead of selling it. The Ig Nobel Prize, a humorous award for research "that makes people laugh and then think," recognized him for teaching people how to endure each other.

cau_hoi: In 1984, engineer Masato Sagawa (Japan) invented the strongest magnet commonly used today, found in electric car motors, headphones, and wind turbines. What alloy is it made from?
giai_thich: Neodymium is a "rare earth" element. A neodymium magnet the size of a coin can lift objects hundreds of times its own weight. Thanks to the strong yet small magnets, motors and speakers can be significantly miniaturized, helping to create compact computer hard drives, phones, and headphones. Vietnam is assessed to have large reserves of rare earth elements in the world.
